We reinforce this with a legal tradition that stretches back to the donation of imperial authority itself, giving us not only the prestige of God's representative but the documented right to intervene in secular affairs, sanction wars, and call the powerful to account before a higher court than any king commands. This standing as both spiritual voice and legal arbiter means that when we recognize a cause as just, allies gather faster and rivals hesitate longer than they would for any purely secular power.

The great popes of our age have transformed Roma from a city of medieval ruins into the most magnificent court in Christendom — commissioning artists, architects, and scholars to fill the Vatican with beauty that will outlast any dynasty and draw the eyes of Europe to the Apostolic See. We build on the bones of the ancient empire deliberately, wrapping our spiritual authority in the prestige of classical civilization and ensuring that every ambassador who enters our city understands he is visiting a power with roots older than any kingdom he serves. This investment in permanent magnificence means our prestige does not diminish with the passing of individual popes, because what we have built speaks for itself long after the man who commissioned it is gone.

The Council of Trent has reformed doctrine and sharpened the institutional boundaries of the Church, but the Papal States themselves remain a patchwork of cities, lordships, and client territories whose local princes have long treated our authority as negotiable. We act now to close that gap — absorbing the revenues, appointments, and legal jurisdictions that local lords have quietly accumulated over generations, and placing them under direct administration from Rome in the manner that the reformed Curia demands. This consolidation of crown authority over our territories gives the Papacy the financial and administrative foundation that the Counter-Reformation's ambitions require.

The Peace of Westphalia has excluded us from the diplomacy of princes, but it has not settled the question of who speaks for the Catholic Church within each Catholic kingdom — a question now pressed with dangerous urgency by those who would make the Church a department of the crown. We assert our primacy over the bishops of France, Germany, and Austria not as a formality but as a living doctrinal reality, condemning the propositions of Gallicanism and forcing clergy who have drifted toward national loyalties to account for the authority they owe to Rome. This reassertion of the Pope's exclusive right to define Catholic doctrine brings wavering churches back under the orthodoxy of the Holy See and restores the flow of tithes and ecclesiastical revenues that national rulers had begun to redirect toward themselves.

The political earthquakes of revolution and war have stripped away much of our temporal power, yet the fundamental need of states for religious legitimacy has not diminished — and it is precisely this need that we leverage in the formal treaties we call Concordats. We negotiate with each sovereign power separately, trading some degree of independence in administrative matters for legally binding recognition of Church rights, the security of our seminaries, and the formal standing of Catholic clergy within their borders. This system of bilateral agreements transforms every Catholic state from a potential adversary into a partner bound by treaty, giving us a diplomatic reach that no army could have preserved.

ref.d: The Holy See is the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Rome, the Pontifex Maximus, head of the Catholic Church, known as The ….

m: Ruler Name Uses Court Language: yes

adv.d: Although the Thai script is already common to all Thai people, it should not be forgotten that it was in our country and under our guidance that it was developed. As such, Thai script is not only a unifying force for our culture, but also proof of our individuality and distinctiveness.

It was not so long ago that we saw ourselves under the Khmer authority, but we have since gained our freedom, and have taken our rightful place as an independent power. We have earned the admiration of our peers, and their respect.

We are called the first independent Thai kingdom, as we were the first ones to rebel against Khmer authority and establish ourselves as free from their influence. As such, all Thai people look at us in admiration.

Most of the history of the early Sukhothai kingdom comes from inscriptions on the Ram Khamhaeng Stele, commissioned by the great king to give a record of his glorious reign. The Ram Khamhaeng Stele is a sacred piece of heritage and one that surely proves our place in history.

We are known for our many gorgeous temples, such as the Wat Si Sawai, one of the oldest in Sukhothai. Built under the Khmer authority as a Hindu temple, its ensuing repurposing has turned it into a symbol of our identity. The faith of our people is strong.

Ceramics have been created by the Thai people since antiquity, influenced by Chinese ceramics but always retaining their own distinct style. However, the ceramics produced in our country are most valued, and they are often traded at great distances overseas.
Our armies have a long history of victory in combat. As a result, a position in our military is seen as a post of honor and prestige, and there are many willing to serve.

Many have tried in the past to stop our progress and expansion, but all have failed in the face of our army. It has proved to be an unstoppable force, one that readily crushes any obstacles in our way.

adv.n: Perpetual General Captain of the People
adv.d: The Scaligeri have claimed the title of Capitano del Popolo not as a temporary office but as a permanent grant rooted in commune law, framing every military campaign as the defense of civic rights rather than dynastic ambition and making it far harder for rivals to cast our wars as mere aggression. Cangrande della Scala built his reputation on exactly this legitimacy — riding out against Milan, Venice, and Padua while presenting each conflict as a just cause — and we formalize his example by keeping the city's councils engaged in decisions that other lords make alone. This combination of legal standing and public mandate makes rivals reluctant to antagonize us openly, since any attack on Verona reads as an attack on the commune itself.

Dante Alighieri spent years of his exile walking our streets, and his presence drew others — poets, scholars, and master builders who found in Verona's Roman ruins and abundant stone a city still worth adding to. We extend this tradition of welcome into deliberate policy, offering patronage to displaced talent and drawing the finest craftsmen to the ancient workshops of the Marmorina, where the stone-cutting skills of generations meet the fresh techniques that newcomers bring from across Italy. This reputation for hospitality draws artists of unusual quality and gives our ambitious construction projects a depth of skilled labor that rivals who must import both talent and stone cannot easily match.

The Adige runs from the Alps through the center of our city and down to the Adriatic, carrying grain, timber, and finished goods along a route that has been profitable since Roman times. We invest in improving the river landings, clearing the shallower stretches, and negotiating passage rights with the communes downstream, turning a natural advantage into a managed commercial system. This continuous river trade fills our markets with goods from the mountains and gives our city a steady prosperity that rivals cannot easily cut off.

Verona's amphitheater is one of the finest surviving Roman monuments in Italy, and we have made it the stage for the greatest public Spettacoli in the north — bullfights, pageants, and civic competitions that draw crowds from Venice and the Terraferma for days at a time. No other city can offer this scale of spectacle inside ancient Roman stone, and the tradition has become inseparable from how Verona understands itself, a republic that still performs its identity before thousands of witnesses in a space built two thousand years ago. This reputation for public magnificence spreads our name across northern Italy and draws visitors whose spending and whose letters home do more for our standing than any envoy we could send.

Verona sits at the point where the road from the Brenner Pass descends into the Po plain, making whoever holds our city the keeper of the most traveled route between Italy and the German lands. We have rebuilt our walls with the full depth of bastioned fortification and maintained the largest permanent garrison in northern Italy. This position means that any army moving south must either take Verona first or leave a hostile city at its back, and we intend to make both choices expensive.

Verona has become a destination that the educated aristocracy of Europe cannot complete their travels without visiting — English lords, French scholars, and German princes make their way to the Arena, the Roman theater, and the Gothic tombs of the Scaligeri, spending freely and writing the city into the correspondence of every court on the continent. Their accounts turn Verona into a byword for Italy's layered heritage, a city where Roman, medieval, and Renaissance civilization can be read in a single afternoon's walk through streets that belong to no single century. This steady stream of wealthy and influential visitors enriches our treasury, opens diplomatic conversations that our size alone would never invite, and builds a reputation for civilization that travels far ahead of our armies.

The Genoese Galley is the backbone of the Genoese navy. Lighter and longer than other galleys used in the Mediterranean Sea, this ship is able to achieve unmatched speed while also having a significant cargo advantage at the cost of maneuverability and durability.

We have built our republic on the twin pillars of commerce and credit, pioneering instruments of debt and exchange that have funded our trading posts from the Levant to the Black Sea since the early Middle Ages. Our colonies and comptoirs across the Mediterranean are as much diplomatic outposts as commercial ones, granting us a reach that no purely military power could match. This network of finance and statecraft ensures our bankers and envoys work as one, reducing the cost of credit and keeping more ambassadors in our service.

Founded to consolidate the mounting debts of the republic, the Casa di San Giorgio has become one of the most sophisticated financial institutions in Christendom. Private creditors and the state share in its governance, channeling Genoese wealth into ventures abroad while keeping the cost of borrowing low. This union of public and private capital gives us unmatched capacity to finance our ambitions.

Genoese Crossbowmen are a respected military unit that was used by the Genoese during the First Crusade up until now. Equipped with Genoese crossbows and the pavise, these infantrymen serve as the protection of their home as well as mercenaries in Europe.

adv.d: In the turbulent years of the early sixteenth century, Andrea Doria restructured our republic, consolidating the old noble factions into twenty-eight great houses — the Aberghi (Alberghi in standard Italian: great houses) — and granting us a political stability we had long been denied. That same pragmatic spirit reshaped our fleet, redirecting our naval expertise toward service across the Mediterranean rather than tying us to a single strategic posture. This reinvention allows us to maintain our navy at reduced cost and to convert our war galleys to lighter vessels when the moment demands it.

The great banking fairs of Piacenza have made Genoese financiers the indispensable creditors of the Spanish crown and the arbiters of European capital flows for generations. The immense wealth that passes through our hands finds its way into the palaces and villas of our merchant nobility, who have built the most far-reaching commercial network in the Mediterranean world. This supremacy over European finance makes our merchant network more efficient than any rival's, and the trade it channels through Genoa fills our treasury with returns drawn from every major commercial circuit in Europe.

The prosperity of centuries of trade has made Genoa a city of collectors and patrons, and from this milieu there has emerged a distinct Genoese School of painting celebrated for its mastery of dramatic light and rich texture. Artists nurtured in our republic have carried Genoese taste and prestige to courts and collections across Europe. This flourishing of artistic culture deepens our traditions and extends our influence far beyond what politics alone can achieve.

As the great Atlantic trade routes have drawn commerce away from the Mediterranean, we have answered by declaring our harbor a Porto Franco — a free port open to merchants of all nations, exempt from the duties and restrictions that weigh down our rivals. Ships that once bypassed Liguria now put in at our quays, and the city fills again with foreign factors, warehouses, and coin. This openness to all comers turns our harbor into one of the busiest entrepôts of the western Mediterranean, drawing trade and people in equal measure.

ref.d: This is the meeting of all the trade associations of Genoa, and the noble lords of the surrounding valleys and coast, joining together to form the city's government.

No man should rule a country alone, or else we are no better than the tyrannical despots who try to subjugate our people. The Capitano del Popolo shall be a dual position where members of the Spinola and Doria families will each hold office. The rivalry between their alberghi keeps the Republic restless, but their Diarchs share the burdens of state and their countinghouses keep the coin flowing.

ref.n: Great and Minor Councils of Genoa
ref.d: Created by Admiral Andrea Doria after reforming the Genoese government, the Great and Minor Councils of Genoa are the two legislative bodies of the state. The Great Council represents the members of the Burghers while the Minor Council is made up of the Nobility.

adv.d: The golden lilies and double-headed eagles of our banners speak to ancient rights and royal ambitions. Claims that stretch across Italy, reaching as far as Albania and Jerusalem, still echo in our hearts. Let the House of Valois-Anjou rise higher than ever before!

A potent mix of Capetian dignity and Angevin ambition courses through our blood. Though we no longer wear the crown of Jerusalem, we remain heirs to a legacy of kingship that once stretched from Anjou to Albania. With careful diplomacy and planning, we may yet revive the grandeur of our forefathers and claim what was unjustly taken from us.

The Rhône Valley has always been our artery of power, and our castles stand watch over it like sentinels of stone. These fortifications are some of the sturdiest in all of Europe, a steadfast sign of our military and engineering prowess, forever watching over our domain.

Toulon's natural harbor offers the ideal staging ground for our naval ambitions. While Marseille thrives as our commercial jewel, Toulon shall be the armory of Provence, and the launching point of a future maritime power.

A series of loosely consolidated laws and statutes form the legal backbone of our governance. These statutes blend Roman jurisprudence with local customs and Angevin tradition, allowing us to manage a patchwork of regions as one cohesive domain: a true composite monarchy, where the parts are diverse, but the crown is indivisible.

Penned by royalty, the 'Book of Tournaments' is more than a manual — it is a statement of courtly pride and chivalric identity. Our nobility trains not only for war but for spectacle, and in doing so preserves martial discipline and prestige across the realm.

Across the workshops of Marseille, artisans stitch delicate boutis quilts in the Provencal style — treasured across Europe for their quality and charm. Much like our duchy, works of art created in our realm are composed of many parts stitched into a unified whole: a quilted land, rich in texture and culture.

The survival of the Nasrid emirate for two centuries past every other taifa rests not on armies but on the agility of our envoys at the courts of Castile, Aragon, the Marīnids, and the Genoese. The kātib al-sirr, our secretary of secrets, maintains a permanent cipher correspondence and a network of merchants doubling as informants from Tunis to Toulouse. This diplomatic infrastructure plays Christian kingdoms against each other through six successive Castilian successions and three Marīnid invasions, buying our emirate decade upon decade of survival.

We descend from the Banū l-Ḵazraj tribe of Yaṯrib through the lineage of Sa'd ibn 'Ubāda, a ṣaḥābī and companion of the Prophet Muḥammad. Our founder Muḥammad I ibn Naṣr, having served first as ally to Ferdinand III, secured the territories of Granada, Jaén, Almería, and Málaga as a tributary emirate after 1238. This dynastic legitimacy, rooted simultaneously in Arab tribal genealogy and prophetic association, gives the Nasrid throne a sacral authority that no Berber successor dynasty in al-'Andalus could ever claim.

The Muṭawwi'a, religiously motivated volunteers from the wider Islamic world, have been coming to Granada since the late thirteenth century to fight a defensive jihad on the last Andalusi frontier. North African Berber riders, Turkish archers passing through Ifriqiya, and Mamlūk-trained officers from Cairo accept Nasrid coin and the promise of paradise to swell our ranks beyond what our small population could ever raise. This pool of volunteer reinforcement lets a kingdom of three hundred thousand subjects field armies whose ferocity surprises every Castilian commander who has not faced them before.

For three centuries Granadan merchants have stood astride the only legal trade channel between the Christian Mediterranean and the gold caravans of the Sahara, exchanging Castilian wool and Genoese silver for Sudanese gold dust at the entrepôts of Málaga and Almuñécar. The Portuguese rounding of Cape Bojador now threatens to bypass us entirely, so we will charter new partnerships with the Wattāsid sultans of Fez and tighten Genoese commercial privileges at our ports. This reorientation of our trade lets the Nasrid economy survive the opening of the African coast that would otherwise have ended our centuries of commercial advantage.

Three generations of Nasrid succession crises — the dethronements of Muḥammad VI, Muḥammad VIII, and Muḥammad IX — have made factional warfare between the Banū as-Sarrāj (the Abencerrajes) and the Banū l-'Aziz the defining feature of court politics. Under a strong emir, the rival clans are confined to ceremonial offices, the Alhambra guard is renewed with loyal Mudejars, and the great vizierate is reserved for men of demonstrated competence rather than blood claim. This dynastic consolidation ends the internal bleeding that has cost us more cities than every Castilian campaign combined.

Al-'Andalus was once the intellectual heart of the Islamic world, producing Ibn Rushd's commentaries on Aristotle, az-Zahrāwī's surgical compendium, and Ibn Ṭufayl's philosophical novel Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān. We will refound the Madrasa Yūsufiyya in Granada, recall scholars from Fez and Tlemcen, and translate the new Spanish and French scientific works into Arabic for the use of our physicians and astronomers. This intellectual revival proves that the lamp of Andalusi learning has only been dimmed, never extinguished, and gives our state a soft-power influence across the Maghreb that no Christian neighbor can replicate.

ref.d: We are the only surviving member of the formerly Muslim realms that populated Al-'Andalus in the past. Huge Muslim empires have risen and fallen throughout Iberia, fragmenting in the process. As one of those fragmented parts, it is our destiny to reunify the people of Iberia under our banner.

adv.d: We have been granted the rulership of Bavaria directly by the Emperor! By embellishing ourselves as the divinely-appointed protectors of Bavaria, we will ensure our legitimacy cannot be questioned.

Our nobles have distinguished themselves as formidable knights in the service of the Holy Roman Empire. We should nurture and scrupulously maintain these troops to ensure the survival of our ducal integrity.
Our lands are rich in the crops and fresh water required to brew beer, and our people readily enjoy this abundance. Many small breweries could grow into successful businesses, with the right support.

Our lands are frequently crossed by merchants wishing to trade Salt, Silver, and Livestock in the rich lands to our south. We would be foolish not to take advantage of their presence, and therefore will establish bustling trade hubs in our own lands to attract their business.

With our homeland at the feet of the beautiful Alps, we are a destination for artists from all over Europe, who seek inspiration in our incredible landscape. If we were to construct and support the appropriate cultural institutions, we could refine our court into a center of refinement and elegance, one that could rival even the most prestigious powers of Europe.
We once were ruled by Bavaria, unified in culture and allied under a single banner. We must ensure that the new Bavarian state is equally mighty, a home worthy of its strong and proud people.
Establishing a council with the sole duty of advising our ruler during times of conflict will help us develop a more capable fighting force.
We must ensure our people remain united in their faith, and that they will not be divided by heretical thoughts.
Only with a formidable standing army will we have the military might necessary to match our ambitions. With careful focus, we can expand it without having a ruinous impact on our state's finances.

No matter if we are answering to an Imperial overlord or cozying up to a potential foreign ally, our diplomats must be prepared for everything. But only if they keep Bavarian interests first and foremost in their efforts will we be able to claim true success in our diplomatic maneuverings.
Our realm needs a new standardized coin to serve as our national unified currency. Establishing a state-owned mint in our capital would ensure our total control over this new coinage.

The excellent quality of our beer has been celebrated for centuries, but for our brews to achieve legendary status, we must ensure their continued prestige and superiority for all time. Several rulers in the past have created regulations and standards for the brewing of this wonderful substance; and we could use this fact as a stamp of our breweries' quality.
The ancient trading ports founded by the Ostmen are still bustling hives of mercantile activity where the canny can get rich.
Our boundary is defined by light defensive works of dykes and palisades designed to deter our unruly neighbors from launching their irritating raids.

Sunda lies at the crossroads of great empires: India, China, and the Islamic world. By positioning ourselves as an indispensable node in this network, we secure access to goods, ideas, and partners across Asia turning our harbors into gateways of prosperity.

The fertile volcanic soil of the Sundanese highlands is perfect for growing the prized spice, black pepper. Traders from across the world seek our peppercorns for their potency and aroma. We must capitalize on this natural treasure to expand our influence through spice.

Held after the harvest, the Sérén Taun festival is an annual thanksgiving ceremony celebrating agricultural abundance. Marked by rituals, offerings, and music, it strengthens the communal bonds of our kampung-kampung and reminds all of the sacred balance between people, rice, and nature.

The foundation of Sundanese society lies in every kampung, rural communities that dot the landscape. Investing in the infrastructure of these villages ensures sustainable growth, strong local leadership, and resilience against both famine and invasion.

Despite its humble origins, the Jaqeli dynasty has been able to establish many successful relationships, forging strong ties to the rulers of surrounding states. As such, we have a positive reputation in the diplomatic sphere.

We are not just one part of the Kingdom of Georgia, as a long time ago we received royal recognition and, with it, the title of Atabeg. This title had previously been granted only to the Armenian vassals, and therefore its conveyance is a sign of distinction and of the respect that the Georgian monarch has for us.

While still a part of Georgia, Samtskhe operates with substantial independence. This privileged position requires constant diplomatic awareness and a policy of active diplomacy, ensuring that we always have a direct channel to those in power. We do all this while actively engaging in our internal politics, meddling with the succession and forging dynastic alliances as best benefits us. The survival of our relatively small state depends on upholding these diplomatic traditions. Let it never be said that we have done too little or acted without sufficient wisdom!

Our mountainous terrain has acted as a shield against foreign invaders many times. Because of this, we learned to build strong fortresses and to always be prepared for defensive warfare. This legacy of strength and readiness is one we must strive at all costs to uphold — the fortresses of Samtskhe must be perpetually well maintained, manned, and supplied, as foreign invaders are not a possibility but a certainty.

Samtskhe has often been obligated to bow to foreign rulers, be they Muslim or Christian; Georgian, Turkic, or Iranian. To build an enduring state that survives as an independent entity and can stand against covetous outsiders, we must establish independent institutions: issuing our own coinage, creating our own laws, and patronizing our own theologians and writers.

The Caucasus have been shaped by nomadic emperors since time immemorial, but the lush pastures of Samtskhe have convinced many tribesmen to settle. We must not let this affect the stability of our kingdom, but instead make arrangements with these settling tribes so that they contribute to our military ambitions in exchange for the lands they claim.

Our position at the crossroads of Georgia, Anatolia, Armenia, and Āzarbāijān also means that a great number of traders seek to cross our lands. However, the constant threat of being raided by nomadic tribesmen means that some have come to doubt the safety of traveling on our roads. We must properly defend all roads and merchant inns in our nation so that trade revenue can flow into our state treasury unhindered.

The lands of Samtskhe are home to places both sacred and revered among the Georgian people. The cave monastery of Vardzia, the ancient church of Atskuri with its miraculous icon of the Virgin Mary, and the Monastery of Ancha with its Anchiskhati icon, are some of the most significant holy places in our realm. By protecting and curating the Samtskhe church, setting it apart as distinct from that of Georgia, we ensure that our people stand united even in the face of adversity.
Our country has always served as a bridge between the Christian and Muslim worlds. As such, people of both faiths within our borders have become accustomed to interacting with each other.
Now that our ties to England have been strengthened, we shall incorporate some of their military tactics, refining our units into fearsome forces.

Since the start of our war against English tyranny, we have preserved our independence through the valiant efforts of the courageous Scottish people. The memory of brave men like William Wallace will motivate our armies to defend and protect Scottish independence for all time!

adv.d: We can consider ourselves to be both members of the traditional lands of the Holy Roman Empire, and of the realm of France. While this can complicate feudal relations, the situation has molded us into adept diplomats, able to skillfully play both sides to our own advantage.
We occupy a prestigious position within the feudal system of France. Therefore, it is only right that our troops are seen as a reflection of the Burgundian spirit.

Our reliance on feudal levies has proven inadequate for the demands of modern warfare. The creation of permanently contracted cavalry units, the Compagnies d'Ordonnance, provides us with a reliable and professional military force directly loyal to the Crown.

The traditional Estates General favors the clergy and nobility, but the rising wealth and political importance of towns can no longer be ignored. By refining its structure to reflect the growing strength of the merchant class, we ensure more balanced governance while preserving the privileges of the other estates. A stronger urban voice will also enhance our administrative capacities and speed up the rate of urbanization.

Burgundy is a feudal creation with various parts conjoined under different conditions, which has created strong local identities. By promoting a central assembly, we give a forum for these interests, promoting a smooth and uncontested rule.

The feudal levy system has proven slow and unreliable in this new age of professional warfare. Inspired by the French model, we will replace our scattered vassal hosts with salaried companies, skilled officers, and integrated armies. A disciplined core of professional soldiers will form the backbone of a modern and adaptable army.

adv.d: One of Europe's foremost chivalric orders. Being a Knight of the Golden Fleece is a mark of great status, and reflects well upon us.

To ensure consistent recruitment and sufficient supply of fighters, we must establish a formal regimental system. This reform will allow us to organize manpower more effectively, centralize command structures, and reduce dependence on local nobles and foreign mercenaries.

The lands of Burgundy are well-suited to growing plants and herding animals. Grapes are particularly apt for local growing conditions. With skilled cultivation, it should be easy to foster an agricultural industry.

From the days of the earliest Doge, Venice has built its power on the mastery of the sea — our merchants carry the riches of the East through the Adriatic while the Stato da Mar, our network of overseas ports and islands, secures the routes that sustain it all. At the heart of this maritime order stands the Arsenale, the greatest industrial complex of the medieval world, capable of launching a fully fitted galley in a single day when the Republic demands it. This combination of merchant dominance, state shipyard, and overseas empire makes Venice unlike any landlocked rival, transforming the sea itself into an extension of our state.

The great palaces rising along our canals embody an architecture wholly our own — borrowing the pointed arch of the Gothic north, the open loggia of the Byzantine east, and the delicate tracery of Islamic craftsmen, fused into the style we call Gotico Fiorito. Nowhere else in Italy does a merchant's wealth announce itself so confidently in stone and carved marble, and the Palazzo Ducale and the Ca' d'Oro stand as proof that our republic can raise monuments as magnificent as any king's. This architectural tradition reinforces the standing of our patrician class, making the physical face of Venice inseparable from the prosperity and civic pride that sustains it.

When Aldo Manuzio established the Aldine Press in Venice in 1494, we became the printing capital of the world almost overnight — our merchants had the gold to finance it, our scholars the Greek and Latin to edit it, and our trade routes to carry the finished books to every court in Europe. The italic typeface, the affordable pocket octavo, and the authoritative editions of Plato, Aristotle, and Virgil that Aldo produced set a standard that no press on the continent has since matched. This mastery of the book trade gives Venice a commercial and intellectual reach that extends far beyond what our galleys can carry, making the ideas that flow from our presses as valuable as the spices in our warehouses.

The twin choir lofts of San Marco, facing each other across the golden nave, gave birth to the Cori Spesâi (Cori Spezzati in standard Italian: Divided Choirs) technique — two ensembles answering and overlapping in a controlled interplay of sound that only the basilica's extraordinary acoustics can fully realize. Adrian Willaert, the Gabrielis, and Claudio Monteverdi all worked within this tradition, and the musicians they trained carried the Venetian polyphonic style to courts from Madrid to Vienna. This school of music makes Venice the acknowledged capital of European sound, and the stream of composers and singers our city produces carries Venetian prestige to places our galleys never reach.

In 1638 the Great Council of Venice took the unprecedented step of licensing a permanent public gambling house in the Palazzo Dandolo, creating the Ridotto — the first state-supervised casino in Europe. Admission required a mask and a patrician's hat, which gave the establishment the appearance of equality while ensuring that the proceeds flowed reliably to the treasury and the behavior of the nobility remained visible to the state. This managed institution transformed a vice the Republic could not suppress into a dependable source of revenue and a mechanism for keeping the city's most powerful men where they could be watched.

The Teatro La Fenice — the Phoenix — opened its doors in 1792 as the grandest opera house in Italy, built to replace a theater lost to fire and named for the bird that rises from its own ashes, a symbol that would prove grimly prophetic more than once. Its gilded interior, its boxes arranged by rank, and its season of premieres turned opera from aristocratic private entertainment into the defining cultural event of a city that had run out of military victories but not beauty. This theater gives Venice a stage on which the Republic's taste, wealth, and ambition are on display every night, reaching an audience of nobles, travelers, and critics whose admiration travels further than any diplomatic dispatch.

ref.d: No city in Europe has confronted the threat of epidemic with more rigor than Venice, and the permanent Magistrato alla Sanità we have established is the most sophisticated public health institution in the world — staffed by physicians, notaries, and inspectors all bound to report the first signs of contagion to a central authority. When plague appears at our borders, the Magistracy holds the power to quarantine arriving ships in the lagoon for forty days, a measure we call quarantina, and impose penalties on anyone who conceals sickness. This system has spared Venice from catastrophes that have emptied rival cities, and it keeps our workforce, our merchants, and our fleet healthy enough to sustain trade even as disease sweeps across the peninsula.

The original lending system in Italy was a joint stock fund called Monte Vecchio, in which each citizen was required to lend a certain amount of money in exchange for interest. But with this updated iteration, our bankers have introduced a guaranteed minimum interest payment to lenders, which has increased the amount of money people are willing to invest. This 'Monte Nuovo' has been extremely successful, and should prove extremely lucrative over time.
The 'Relazioni' are the reports our ambassadors send to the government, detailing the political, financial, and social state of the countries they serve in.

The mainland territories of the terraferma hold agricultural potential that poor drainage, neglect, and feudal indifference have left unrealized — marshes that could be grain fields, river banks that flood each spring and wash away the labor of the season before. We have established the Provveditori ai Beni Inculti with the authority to commission drainage canals, enforce irrigation schemes, and compensate landowners whose cooperation the works require. This systematic land improvement has extended the productive capacity of our wealthiest agricultural regions, giving Venice a food surplus that keeps the city fed even when sea trade is disrupted by war or blockade.

adv.d: The feudal laws of the Frankish East are the most refined in the Catholic world, having been codified to manage a complex web of Greek serfs and French lords. These Assizes provide a clear legal framework for land disputes, inheritance, and military obligations, ensuring that even in times of war, the social order remains unbreakable. Rigorous adherence to these laws prevents the internal fractures that destroyed the first Crusader states, providing a rock-solid foundation for governance.

The Peloponnese remains the heart of European silk production, a legacy of the Byzantine era that the Frankish Princes have expanded through state-sponsored mulberry groves. By controlling strategic ports, we can undercut the high prices of Persian and Chinese imports, making Achaea the primary supplier for the garment makers of Florence and Lyon. This monopoly provides a steady stream of Soft Gold that funds our mercenaries and the fortification of our mountain passes.

Our nobility has spent centuries in constant border skirmishes against our enemies, creating a unique tradition of highly mobile cavalry. These knights have discarded the cumbersome barding of their French ancestors in favor of lighter armor and tactics adapted for the steep, treacherous Greek mountains. This allows our forces to outmaneuver traditional heavy cavalry and strike at the enemy's flanks with devastating speed and precision.

Our coastal defenses are unmatched, utilizing Italian Trace Italienne design to repel enemy naval raids and incursions into our sovereign territory. We have transformed the old Crusader castles into modern artillery forts, capable of withstanding months of siege while projecting power over the Ionian and Aegean seas. No invader shall take the Morea by sea so long as our stone sentinels stand watch over the rocky capes and fertile valleys.

As scholars flee the crumbling peripheries of the East, many find refuge in our courts, leading to a unique synthesis of Latin philosophy and Greek classical knowledge. Under the enlightened patronage of the Princes, we have established academies where the works of the great sages of both East and West are studied side-by-side, sparking a cultural rebirth. This intellectual flowering attracts the best minds of Europe, ensuring our state remains at the cutting edge of administrative and scientific progress.

Geoffrey of Villehardouin, marshal of Champagne and eyewitness chronicler of the Fourth Crusade, composed one of the earliest vernacular histories in Old French, immortalizing the deeds of his companions and the astonishing capture of Constantinople in vivid, heroic prose that circulated widely among the nobility of Western Europe. His chronicle served not only as a record but as propaganda and inspiration, rallying fresh knights and pilgrims to reinforce the beleaguered Latin states, while fostering a shared sense of chivalric brotherhood among the scattered Frankish lords who continued to view themselves as crusaders holding God's frontier against schismatic and infidel alike long after the original host had dispersed. It is time to recover that spirit for the challenges of our army.
