adv.d: The Flemish Cloth industry is the envy of the world. Merchants come from far away to sell their Wool in Flanders, where we manufacture the best quality Cloth.

As one of the most prosperous regions on the continents, much of the wealth we have created naturally flows toward artistic patronage. Flemish merchants commission master painters to create art that, while perhaps not practical, casts light over even the cloudiest of days. With dozens of our merchants actively hiring artists and commissioning new pieces, we are creating a distinctive Renaissance of our own.

As our cloth, luxury goods, and financial industries face growing competition, it is becoming obvious that we need to manage our land use better. By creating regional granaries, we further diversify our economy, and bolster our food stores against famine or poor harvests.

Our unique sea-meets-oasis geography, with palm groves growing within sight of the Mediterranean shore on the Gulf of Gabes, supports a rare combination of date-palm production, citrus orchards, henna gardens, and Mediterranean fishing in the same agrarian unit. Our peasants harvest dates in autumn, sail for tuna in spring, and trade across both the Saharan and the Mediterranean trade-circuits without ever leaving our oasis hinterland. This coastal-oasis geography gives our state a fruit-output ceiling and a steady prosperity that purely-inland oases cannot match.

Our natural harbor on the Gulf of Gabes, sheltered by the Kerkennah islands, deep enough for Mediterranean galleys, and supplied with fresh water from the oasis itself, supports a fleet of coastal galleys and a sailor-pool drawn from our oasis-and-coast inhabitants in equal measure. Our shipwrights train in the techniques of both the eastern-Mediterranean galley-building and the Saharan caravan-camel husbandry that our hinterland requires. This Gulf-anchorage geography gives our state a steady sailor recruitment and a navy-tradition that purely-inland oases or purely-coastal cities cannot replicate.

Our coastal-oasis henna gardens, indigo plots, and saffron fields produce the dyes that European cloth-finishers and Maghrebi tanneries demand in the highest grades — supplying the colorants for Andalusi-style tilework, Mediterranean wool-dyeing, and our own coastal cotton industries. Our merchant houses control the bonded warehouses at the Gulf shore, our brokers extend credit to the dye-grove owners, and our shipping agents route the export through Tunis, La Goulette, and the smaller Tunisian ports. This dye-export industry gives our crown a luxury-export revenue and a merchant-maintenance efficiency that purely-pastoral oases cannot match.

Our crown develops the date-export economy of the Gulf coastline, sinking new artesian wells, extending the palm groves along the coastal plain, and laying paved roads that link Gabes, Djerba, and the smaller coastal markets to the central oasis. With each expansion the shared infrastructure lowers the cost of working the land across the coastal-oasis hinterland. This coastal development gives our state a farming and road network that the inland oases, cut off from the sea, cannot match.

Our salt-flat works at the edge of the Chott el-Djerid, the great seasonal salt-pan stretching inland from the Gulf of Gabes, supply the Mediterranean-and-Saharan salt trade with grades from coarse industrial salt to the fine table-salt our coastal evaporation produces. Our salt-houses, our scale-houses, and our customs posts route every load through bonded accounting, and our central treasury captures revenue from both ends of the salt-trade chain. This salt-economy gives our crown a salt-output ceiling and a steady tax-efficiency that purely-agricultural oases cannot match.

Our tight commercial bond with the island of Djerba, sustained by daily fishing-and-trade traffic across the narrow Gulf of Gabes channel, extends our merchant network across the Mediterranean basin through the Djerba-resident Sephardic, Genoese, and Maltese commercial houses. Our agents conduct business in every Mediterranean port through Djerba intermediaries, our shipping factors coordinate with the Djerba pilot-houses, and our customs posts capture revenue from both the island and the mainland traffic. This Djerba-link gives our state a trade-sea efficiency and a merchant-capacity reach that purely-inland coastal cities cannot replicate.

The tusks of the walrus and the pelts of the arctic fox are among the finest goods that Greenland can offer the world. Our merchants brave the cold waters to bring these treasures to the markets of Europe, and in doing so keep our colony alive and prosperous.

Our forefathers sailed westward from these icy shores and discovered Vinland, a land of plenty far across the ocean. The memory of those voyages lives on in our sagas, and we know the route our ancestors took. Let us sail west once more and reclaim what was once ours.

The shores of Vinland are within our reach. We have the knowledge of the route, the ships to sail it, and the will to endure the crossing. Let us establish a permanent presence in the west and use Greenland as the launchpad for a new era of settlement.

The Greenlandic waters teem with whales, seals, and fish. Our hunters have perfected the art of reading the ice and the tides, and their mastery of the sea keeps our people fed and our ships manned. There is no finer school for a sailor than the waters of the north.

The crowns of Europe have recognized Greenland as a land worth investing in. A formal charter organizes our trade under royal authority, attracting merchants from across Europe and ensuring that the wealth of the north flows through Greenlandic ports rather than around them.

Generations of Greenlandic navigators have mapped every current, ice shelf, and hidden passage in the waters around our shores. This knowledge, compiled into charts of unmatched precision, makes Greenland an indispensable partner for any expedition venturing into the northern seas.
During our time as subjects of Mali, our people learned much from their military command and combat tactics. This knowledge shall help our own infantry in battles to come.

Before the Malian Empire came to dominate Western Africa, the city of Gao was the capital of an empire in its own right. Although there are barely any written records of the Gao Empire, its legacy lives on in our oral traditions, inspiring all who want to achieve greatness one day.

Some say that Salt is worth its weight in Gold... perhaps it would be more accurate to say that Gold is worth its weight in Salt. Either way, by exchanging these two commodities, we have established thriving trade networks.

For many years, we were a subject of Mali. As Mali's power has weakened, ours has grown, and we can now claim to be fully independent of Malian overlordship. Let us take steps to make sure we remain so.

Despite the best efforts of centuries of Sunni sultanates, Western Africa is still plagued by the menace of Animistic pagans. By lifting the banner of Jihād, we can cleanse our lands of the unbelievers and expand our frontiers at the same time.

We have been told that the Sankoré Mosque's school is the greatest center for learning in the entirety of Africa. Who could be surprised if this were true, given how many wise men from distant Arabia and the Maghreb are here right now, arguing the finer points of philosophy and religion?

The Holy Law that the Prophet followed when ruling Madīna should be the unshakable foundation of the laws we use to run our society. By reforming our criminal code to reflect the teachings of the Prophet, we will bring harmony and justice to our people.

Like Mansa Mūsā of Mali once did, our rulers can travel to Mecca on pilgrimage, fulfilling the fifth pillar of Islam and bearing gold as a symbol of our wealth and power. Like the Malian pilgrims of old, the world will gasp in wonder at the wealth and grandeur of Songhai.
Our traders frequently bring back fascinating things from the courts of North Africa. Perhaps they could find and bring back yet more fascinating trinkets?

Our state lives and dies by the capabilities of our army. Our military not only ensures our survival, but is also what has set us on the path to greatness. We cannot allow ourselves to fall behind in progress!

Aquileia was once the fourth city of the Roman Empire and later the seat of a patriarchate that claimed authority over the whole of northeastern Italy and the eastern Alps, a tradition of ecclesiastical prestige that lingered in our institutions long after the political power that created it had passed. We draw on this heritage to build institutions of learning that reflect the city's ancient role as a center of transmission between the Latin west and the Slavic and Germanic east. This tradition of the Patriarchate of Aquileia as a crossroads of cultures and books gives our state an unusual depth of literacy and a tolerance rooted in centuries of managing Christians of different rites under a single ecclesiastical roof.

Long before the Roman legions formalized it, the route that carried Baltic amber from the northern seas down to the Adriatic ran through our territory, making Aquileia one of the great entrepôts of the ancient world and establishing trade habits that outlasted the empire which later paved the road. We revive and invest in this corridor, improving the roads and staging posts that connect our city to the Alpine passes and the trading networks beyond them, ensuring that our merchants can reach markets to the north with greater efficiency than any rival route. This control over the Amber Road multiplies our diplomatic reach and makes our trading lanes the preferred route for goods moving between the Adriatic and central Europe.

Our territory sits at the junction of the Julian Alps and the Karst plateau, a landscape that provides natural defensive advantages to those who know how to use it and proves lethal to armies that do not. We invest in the fortification of the key passes and valley approaches, training our garrison forces to hold terrain rather than meet the enemy in open ground, and establishing a network of signal stations that ensures no advance can reach us without warning. This system of Difesa Alpina makes our territory one of the most costly to invade in the region, converting the rugged landscape into an ally that inflicts losses on any hostile force before our own soldiers need to engage.

The Friulian countryside has always been a frontier, and the men raised on its farmsteads and in its market towns carry a soldier's habits from youth — accustomed to bearing arms, experienced in the local terrain, and under no illusions about what happens to those who cannot defend themselves on a border that hostile powers have crossed many times. We formalize this martial tradition by organizing, equipping, and training the Milizia Friulana on a professional footing, giving these experienced men the discipline and the leadership that converts their individual hardiness into a reliable military force. This soldiery gives our armies a core of steady infantry who fight for their own soil and hold their ground with a tenacity that mercenary formations rarely match.

For centuries, the patriarchs of Aquileia administered a territory that stretched from the Adriatic coast to the Alpine passes, managing ecclesiastical law, civil disputes, and diplomatic relations with secular powers simultaneously — an administrative experience that accumulated in our institutions long after the patriarchate's temporal power was absorbed by Venice. We draw on this heritage to rationalize and improve our own machinery of government, applying the procedural knowledge of an institution that once governed a far larger and more complex territory to the more manageable scale of our current state. This Patriarchal Legacy of administrative sophistication makes our cabinet more effective and our legislation more coherent, giving us a governmental capacity that belies the modest size of our domain.

The memory of Aquileia as a crossroads between west and east, between the Roman and the Slavic worlds, and between the Latin and the Germanic, has given our institutions an instinctive openness to ideas from outside that more homogeneous states can struggle to achieve. We build on this tradition by welcoming the scholars and administrators produced by the Enlightenment into our governing institutions, reforming our laws by the same principles of reason and evidence that the patriarchate once applied to canon law in a different era. This spirit of the Patriarcato illuminato earns our state a reputation as a place where ideas are taken seriously and institutions are genuinely open to improvement, drawing scholars and skilled administrators whose presence accelerates every reform we attempt.

The Four Quartiers are the four provinces into which the core of Brabant is divided. Each quartier is formed by a satellite of large and smaller towns, some walled and others not. They all work in perfect synergy like a well-greased engine, filling our coffers with great riches.

As other nations have, it is time to codify the liberties of our subjects, in order to identify and safeguard their rights and motivate them to continue working towards a better future for our country.

With the foundation of the University of Leuven, Brabant has placed itself firmly at the center of culture in the Netherlands. Students from all over Europe come to our lands to study and share their knowledge.

ref.d: The Joyous Entry grants liberties to our Burghers, akin to a Magna Carta for the Low Countries. This document upholds freedoms for the church, towns, and Nobility, emphasizing consent for taxes and commitments to our nation's indivisibility.

adv.d: By erecting multiple castles in key positions along the Rhine, we will be able to exert and expand our control over both the river and the trade flowing through it.

Originating from the dynastic coat of arms of the Wittelsbach family, the Palatine Lion is the centerpiece of our legitimacy. Displayed with a red crown, it signifies our role as the Imperial Vicar and Arch-Steward of the Holy Roman Empire. As long as the Palatine Lion is proudly displayed on our crest, our legitimacy will not come into question.

By virtue of having our territories disperse, we are vunerable to attacks from several foreign powers. Constructing many fortified outposts within our lands will buy us time to raise an army and repel any attempt to take over one of our many disconnected territories.

u.t: Chivalric order: Society with the Donkey

adv.d: Founded to protect knightly interests within the Empire, the Gesellschaft mit dem Esel has entrenched itself in the lands surrounding Heidelberg. Their expertise in governance, as well as their ability to sponsor tourneys, will improve our cultural standing.

adv.n: Vineyards and Orchards of the Rhine
adv.d: Although our territory is small, the sunny banks of the Rhine are perfectly suited to cultivate vineyards and orchards. With some effort, these could sustain our local economy by producing wine.
The only effect of bloodshed is to cause further bloodshed. Therefore, we need to be a forgiving ruler, and reconcile with our enemies to establish a lasting peace in our territories.

Our administration is skilled in handling multiple disconnected territories without losing our grasp on them. With that, we can build a strong bureaucracy capable of handling even the most difficult tasks.

When our peasantry rises up against our nobility, they unmistakably rise up against our own rule. However, we should not excessively punish those who revolt. With mild consequences, everyone will be more in alignment with our authority.
The Reformation has created many discussions around the nature of our faith. We should invest into a comprehensive catechism, to which our people will be able to adhere.

To govern well, our rulers must receive a comprehensive education in humanist ideas. To this effect, we must hire renowned humanists for the education of our rulers and heirs, while also focusing our court on these principles.

No matter their denominations, all Christian people must be welcomed in the towns and cities of our lands. While others may decide to suppress their religious minorities, our tolerance will ensure a steady stream of immigrants into our territory, and we shall benefit from their presence.

Rich in theological scriptures of several Christian denominations, the Bibliotheca Palatina is one of our most prized possessions. Protection of the knowledge and the cultural value contained within must be a high priority, so that we are able to keep relying on its documents.
A significant part of the Romantic movement is centered around Heidelberg. We should capitalize on this phenomenon, and support these and other artists in order to bolster our global recognition.

The tomb of 'Uqba ibn Nāfi' — founder of Kairouan, who led the first Arab armies into the Maghreb and is buried at our southern village of Sidi Okba — anchors a sacred-pilgrimage site whose religious authority predates every dynasty of the Maghreb. Our resident shrine-keepers maintain the tomb, our annual pilgrimage draws zawaya-scholars and notables from across the western Islamic world, and our ulema invoke the founder's authority in legal opinions that bind clients far beyond our actual political reach. This founding-shrine site gives our polity a sacred-legitimacy claim that no other Maghrebi polity can match for antiquity and prophetic-conqueror anchorage.

Our oasis-belt, the Zībān palm gardens stretching from Biskra and Tolga through Sidi Okba and Bou Saada to Ouled Djellal, produces the dates that the Maghrebi and trans-Saharan markets specifically commission for their size, sweetness, and keeping qualities. Our orchard-owners hold hereditary leases on individual palm plots, our irrigation guildsmen apportion well-water by ancient share-tables, and our caravan-masters price each consignment by origin grove and harvest year. This Zibane palmery gives our oasis polity a niche-luxury revenue stream that no broader fruit-producing region of the Maghreb can displace from the elite markets.

Our oasis sits at the northern terminus of the western Saharan caravan corridor. Caravans from Touat, Touggourt, and the central Sahara converge on Biskra before continuing north to Constantine and Tunis or east into Hafsid territory, while our merchant-houses provision the southbound legs with grain, cloth, salt, and pottery from the Tell. Our caravanserais host sub-Saharan, Berber, and Maghrebi traders side by side; our customs officers tax through-traffic at modest rates that keep the corridor profitable; and our diplomatic letters bind the caravan-route's contributing tribes to our chamber-arbitration. This Saharan-terminus role gives our oasis polity a merchant-capacity and a diplomatic reach that no purely-agricultural oasis could otherwise sustain.

The foggāra underground-channel system, qanats dug under the desert sand to bring water from upland water tables to the oasis gardens, gets extended and renewed under our oasis-council coordination, freeing new cultivable land from the older surface-irrigation perimeter. Our guild of foggara-diggers passes the channel-construction technique through hereditary apprenticeship, our resident villages contribute corvée-labor for the channel-cleaning rotations, and our oasis-chamber arbitrates the share-water disputes that the new channels inevitably generate. This foggara-irrigation expansion gives our oasis polity a cultivable-land-and-population base that the purely-surface-irrigated rival oases cannot match.

The annual Biskra autumn-fair, convening Saharan caravans from Touat, Sahel merchants from Constantine, sub-Saharan slave-traders from the Niger bend, and Bedouin pastoralists from the steppe-fringe, turns our oasis-capital into a regional commercial hub for the autumn weeks. Our pavilions host the negotiations, our customs-house weighs and registers every transaction, and our merchant-guild posts standard scales and assay-weights to which all participants must conform. This Biskra-fair institution gives our oasis a periodic-commerce concentration that turns the natural caravan-confluence into a state-managed revenue event.

The Raḥmāniyya tariqa, founded by Sīdī Muḥammad ibn 'Abd ar-Raḥmān al-Azharī in the central-Kabyle region and expanding southward through the Aurès foothills, establishes branch-zawiyas across our oasis-belt over the course of generations. Our resident shayḵs accept Raḥmāniyya initiation, our scholar-families take students from the Kabyle and central Algerian centers, and our merchant-pilgrims maintain the cross-regional correspondence that binds the order's geographically-dispersed nodes into a coherent religious network. This Raḥmāniyya expansion gives our oasis polity a religious-cultural bridge to the central Algerian highlands that the purely-Saharan Sufi orders cannot supply.
The Paik System is a corvée labor system where capable adults, the so-called Paiks, are obligated to serve in the state militia in exchange for farmland.
Paiks are foot soldiers of India who are renowned for their offensive and defensive versatility and their skill in archery.

Paiks are foot soldiers of India who are renowned for their offensive and defensive versatility and their skill in archery. As the weapons develop, so does their portfolio of skills. Thus, the bows of the early eras have been replaced by the modern musket, yet their versatility still prevails.

In the rugged, rain-swept peaks of the Pindus mountains, the Despots of Epirus have carved out a sanctuary that no Latin army can penetrate. We have mastered the art of 'mountain-ambush' warfare, using the vertical geography of our realm to trap and destroy much larger forces in narrow defiles. This environmental mastery turns our entire country into a deathtrap for invaders, ensuring that while the plains may fall, the mountains remain forever Greek.

Epirus sits at the crossroads of the Greek, Slavic, and Latin worlds, and we have turned our royal daughters into our most effective diplomats. Through a complex web of strategic marriages with Serbian Kings, Albanian Chieftains, and even Italian Counts, we have made the House of Doukas-Komnenos the indispensable arbiter of Balkan politics. These blood-ties ensure that when we go to war, we are never without powerful allies willing to strike from our enemies' flanks.

To bolster our dwindling numbers, we have invited the fierce Arvanite clans to settle in the fertile valleys of Epirus and Acarnania. In exchange for land and autonomy, these warriors provide us with a tireless light infantry force that excels in the brutal, close-quarters combat of the Balkan frontier. Their unique martial culture, blended with our Roman military tradition, creates a hybrid force that is both exceptionally loyal and terrifyingly aggressive in the shock of battle.

By securing the ports of Valona and Butrint, Epirus sits as the warden of the Adriatic Sea. We have leveraged this position to negotiate favorable trade treaties with Venice and the Italian city-states, who must pass through our sphere of influence to reach the Levant. By levying precise tariffs and providing 'protection' services against corsairs, we have transformed our once-isolated despotate into a wealthy commercial hub that bridges the gap between East and West.

The city of Ioannina has been transformed into a true stronghold. Utilizing the latest in Italian military engineering, we have surrounded our capital and its lake with a series of interlocking bastions and water-forts that can withstand months of sustained bombardment. This defensive network serves as the anchor for our entire national strategy, allowing us to retreat into an impregnable core whenever the tides of war turn against us in the open field.

Centuries of survival between powerful enemies have made our diplomatic corps the most sophisticated in the world. We have developed a 'neutrality-of-strength' doctrine, playing the great powers against one another so skillfully that they compete for our favor rather than seeking our conquest. Our ambassadors are renowned for their ability to weave peace treaties that always seem to leave Epirus with more territory and influence than when the conflict began.

The great Luxembourg dynasty, whose very name is derived from that of our nation, is now the most important family in Europe. This has to be a sign from Heaven, and we will use this divine benediction to further extend our influence.

The impregnable position of Luxembourg, with the formation of the Bock acting as a natural fortress, is incredibly strong. Our enemies would perish in any attempt to usurp our holdings. We shall learn from nature, and construct all our fortresses so as to use the local terrain to their advantage.

John the Blind, the heroic King of Bohemia and Count of Luxembourg, was born in our humble realm. He died in the Battle of Crécy at fifty, having charged headlong into combat despite his blindness. His brave, honorable death will inspire our soldiers for centuries.

Savoy has been ruled by a stable line of dynastic counts ever since its creation. By ensuring the unity of our ruling family and maintaining a strong connection to local representatives, we keep our land from being fractured.

Nestled in the high Alps, We are a mountain people before we anything. Their therrain and the passes crossing them are our inheritance, our livelihood, and the mountains themselves are our protectors. Generations of living inside the Alps have given our people an unmatched understanding of their heights and geography.

Our realm is in the possession of a most holy artifact, a piece of cloth that bears the face of Jesus of Nazareth. Naturally, it has attracted numerous pilgrims, all clamoring to see and venerate this extraordinary relic. This constant stream of pilgrimage brings a great deal of wealth into our territory — which is all very much to our advantage.

The passage over the Alps is troublesome at the best of times, and can be outright impossible with carriages or a larger entourage. By maintaining good pathways, shelters, and waystations, we will be able to dominate the difficult terrain and ensure a steady exchange of merchants throughout our territory.
We have embraced the teachings of the Waldensian movement and are dedicated to protecting this faith from the vicious Catholic Church, which seeks to eradicate its ideas.

Our lands have long suffered under the heretical preaching of the Waldensians. By the force of our will and with the support of the divine, we have been able to contain their influence, and we shall continue to defend the one true faith from these dangerous ideas.

Many people in our realm leave the alpine valleys they were born into to settle in the urban areas on either side of the mountain range. This depopulation leaves the small villages of lesser valleys in a precarious, politically unstable position. We must ensure that the valley lands are sufficiently populated and can be adequately maintained.

Our lands are at risk of invasion from hostile neighbors, who desire the riches of our valleys. Creating and funding an order of knights, ready to defend our lands, allows us to draw on greater forces if the need ever arises.
Our people are highly adapted to traverse the obstacles of our country, from the high peaks and passes of our mountains to the wide rivers of our valleys.

Given our location at the center of all Europe, we must adopt a highly flexible attitude towards external diplomacy. Alliances and rivals can shatter as easily as they are formed, and our diplomats must be trained to cover every possible position.
Only well-rounded tactics of artillery shock, cavalry charges, and unyielding infantry recruited from the landknechte can lead us to victory.

ref.d: We have been granted the Privilegium Maius, which grants us an elevated position among the princes of the Holy Roman Empire. This shows our status and prestige even outside of Imperial lands, and elevates us to a higher position than that of a mere duke.

src.n: The Privilegium Maius in Our Hands

adv.d: Our confederation thrives on the transhumant pastoralism of the Tellian Atlas. Sheep, goats, and camels move seasonally between the upland summer pastures of the Aurès and the winter lowlands of the Constantine plain, sustained by a kinship economy that purely-agricultural states cannot replicate. Our tribal chiefs hold their authority through the seasonal grazing-rights they negotiate among the constituent clans, and our pastoral wealth supports a tribal-warrior class whose flocks travel as both wealth and rations. This pastoral foundation gives our state a steady tribesmen-loyalty and a prosperity that the rain-fed agricultural economies cannot easily match.

Our confederation occupies the immediate hinterland of the great fortress-city of Constantine, supplying the city's grain, wool, leather, and livestock markets while our chiefs negotiate caravan-protection and toll-immunity treaties with whichever power holds the city. Our merchant houses ride the constant trade of the Constantine markets, and our envoys gain experience negotiating with the central courts of Algeria and Tunisia alike. This hinterland-of-a-great-city geography gives our state a merchant-capacity reach and a diplomatic experience that purely-mountain confederations far from urban markets cannot replicate.

Our mounted light-cavalry — drawn from the youngest sons of every clan, mounted on the swift Berber horses our pastoral economy raises — patrol the contested frontiers of our confederation, riding down rival raiders, extracting tribute from passing caravans, and gathering reputation in the cross-clan competitive games of the seasonal fairs. Our cavalry tradition transmits its tactical knowledge through hereditary apprenticeship within the warrior families. This raiding tradition gives our state a light-cavalry power and an army-tradition recovery that the more sedentary Maghrebi states cannot reproduce through formal training.

The maraboutic shayḵs of the Aurès, descended from the early-medieval saints whose tombs anchor our highest pilgrimage sites, bind our scattered villages and our wandering pastoralist clans to a single religious-judicial network whose authority no purely-secular chieftaincy can match. Our crown endows the lodge-shrines, our chiefs receive their ijāza from the Aurès shayḵs, and our religious establishment gains the depth that comes from hereditary scholarly succession. This Aurès-anchored religious authority gives our state a clergy-satisfaction baseline and a governmental legitimacy that flatland courts pursuing the same legitimacy cannot easily duplicate.

Our distinctive Tellian Berber dialect, preserving features of the older Zenata speech that the surrounding Arab-Berber synthesis has dissolved elsewhere, anchors our scholarly tradition through the manuscripts of our Aurès qādīs and the religious poetry of our marabouts. Our literate clergy preserves dialect dictionaries, religious-poetry manuscripts, and tribal-history chronicles that the more Arabized neighboring confederations have lost. This linguistic-cultural distinction gives our state a clergy-literacy ceiling and a religious-cultural confidence that the more centralized lowland courts cannot replicate.

Our late-period printers and lithographers at the Aurès market-towns publish bilingual Berber-Arabic periodicals, religious tracts, and tribal-history chronicles, circulating our distinctive cultural identity through the literate Maghrebi reading public. We engage in dialogue with the wider Arab-Islamic reformist movements while preserving our confederation's particular linguistic and ritual inheritance. This bilingual press revival binds our scattered confederation into a shared modern identity and extends our pop-assimilation and conversion reach across the wider Tellian region.

Millions of date palms across the Tuat oases, sustained by the foggāra irrigation networks running tens of kilometers under the desert sand, feed our people, our caravans, and our export trade in equal measure. Our cultivators have selected the celebrated Deglet Nour and Aghras varieties for premium markets across the Mediterranean and the Sahel. This deep oasis cultivation gives our crown a fruit-export volume and a steady prosperity that the rain-fed agriculture of the Maghrebi coast can never match.

Muḥammad al-Maghīlī of Tuat, author of the Aḥkām Ahl adh-Dhimma and counselor to the askiyas of Songhai, exports our Mālikī jurisprudence across the western Sahara, the Hausa cities, and the Sahel kingdoms beyond. His rulings on dhimmī status, taxation, and ruler-subject obligations bind the courts of Songhai, Kano, and Katsina to Tuat's juridical authority. This concentrated scholarly authority extends our cultural influence well beyond our oasis frontiers and binds the southern Maghrebi-Sahelian clergy to our shayḵs.

The Tuat escort companies — armed and mounted on oasis-bred camels and Saharan horses — hire out their services to every major caravan transiting our territory between Sijilmāsa and the Niger bend. Our riders know every waterhole, every reliable forage track, and every raider's likely ambush point across two thousand kilometers of desert. This light-cavalry tradition gives our crown a rapid escort capacity and a campaign-reinforcement speed that the inland Maghrebi powers cannot match without our local knowledge.

Mālikī majority and Ibāḍī minority share the foggāra water-rights, the caravan-protection corps, and the ksar councils across the Tuat oases, a religious coexistence no urban Maghrebi capital can equal under its own jurists' rulings. Our shayḵs of both schools attend the same federation assembly, sit on the same trade-arbitration tribunal, and recognize each other's marriage and inheritance contracts. This pluralistic religious settlement gives our court a tolerance ceiling and a broad religious legitimacy that single-school states perpetually struggle to maintain.

The Tuat caravan-houses (Kawāsim, Bū Bakr, Kuntī) formalize their trans-Saharan monopoly through bonded warehouses at every relay-post, fixed tariffs published at the oasis gates, and exclusive escort contracts that competitors cannot reproduce. Our agents at Walāta, Timbuktu, Sijilmāsa, and Touggourt clear every load through the same set of accounting books. This integrated commercial oligopoly gives our crown a merchant capacity and a tariff revenue that the unorganized caravan-broker towns of the wider Sahara cannot replicate.

As Atlantic steamships divert the gold-and-slave trade away from the desert routes in the late nineteenth century, the Tuat houses pivot to dates, salt, and Saharan-tourist transit, adapting our infrastructure to the smaller but durable commercial niche that survives the steam revolution. Our oases now host visiting foreign scholars, merchant agents, and curious travelers whose payments and gifts supplement the surviving caravan revenues, and our agents at Algiers and Oran open Mediterranean-sea connections to the coastal steamer lines. This adaptive commercial pivot gives our crown a residual sea-trade reach and an urban migration draw that pure-trade-volume Saharan towns could never preserve.

Utrecht, often called the City of Churches, is home to the iconic Dom Tower. The spiritual center of the Netherlands and the seat of the Bishopric of Utrecht, it has been a beacon of faith since antiquity.

The Pope himself influences the election of our Prince-Bishop, challenging the traditional five-chapter election format that we had before. This is clear proof that our land has been divinely blessed!
Given the growing influence of our neighbors, our nation's survival depends on our ability to find loyal, powerful allies who will support us in our times of need.

ref.d: The Judicate is a unique type of government which is defined by its republic-like institutions, and by electing the ruler from within the Supreme Court.

c.t: Is or was the country Arborea (ARB)

adv.d: We have expanded the cultivation of sugarcane in the fertile Messara plain, building advanced water-powered mills (Trapete) for refining. Cretan sugar is now a luxury sought after by the courts of Europe, competing directly with the products of the Levant. This industrial-scale agriculture provides the crown with the gold needed to fund its naval supremacy.

adv.n: The Galley Assembly Line of Suda
adv.d: By standardizing the parts used in the construction of light galleys at Suda Bay, we have pioneered an early form of modular shipbuilding. This allows us to replace lost vessels at a fraction of the time and cost of other Mediterranean powers. A ship built in Candia is recognized for its speed and its ability to navigate the treacherous currents of the Cretan Sea.

The sun-drenched slopes of Mount Ida produce the famed Malvasia grape, which has become the most coveted dessert wine in the royal courts of Northern Europe. By strictly regulating the quality and the Seal of Saint Mark on every barrel exported, we have created a high-value trade monopoly that funds our naval defense. This liquid gold ensures that even as a colony, Candia remains the most profitable jewel in the Venetian maritime empire.

As new threats loom larger, the engineers of the nation have transformed the entire island into a maritime bastion of the Trace Italienne style. By reinforcing the walls of Candia, Rethymno, and Chania with earthworks capable of absorbing heavy cannon fire, we ensure that every siege becomes a multi-decade ordeal for the invader. This infrastructure allows a small garrison to hold out indefinitely against a numerically superior foe while awaiting relief from the sea.

adv.n: The Council of the Two Peoples
adv.d: The constant threat of external invasion and internal revolt led the Latin Kings of Candia to abandon the strict segregation of the early conquest. We have established a 'Great Council' where the ancient Venetian-descended nobility sits alongside the Archontes (the Greek Orthodox landowning elite). This shared governance allows for a unified administrative front, where the military traditions of the West are funded by the deep roots of the local Greek bureaucracy, ensuring the island remains a stable and indigestible bastion for any would-be conqueror.

The fierce Cretan mountain dwellers have been integrated into a professional light cavalry corps, blending Western discipline with the hit-and-run tactics of the Balkan frontier. We have established permanent training grounds where the sons of the local nobility and the Latin settlers learn the art of the Saber and Carbine to protect the island's interior. These units are now exported as elite mercenaries to many states, providing a steady stream of military prestige and revenue.

u.t: Chivalric order: Order of Saint Hubert

adv.d: The Hubertusorden will serve as a glorious reminder of our knights' combat prowess! Joining the order will be a reward for our loyal knights, and its members will display our glory for all to see.

Not so long ago, our city was nearly torn apart in the struggle between our burghers and our clergy. We must ensure that this conflict cannot repeat itself, and that every member of both our court and the city council cooperate in preserving Cologne as a central hub on the Rhine.

Our city is home to many capable painters and craftsmen skilled in the art of bringing images to life through the media of wood, stone, and especially glass. With the support of a strongly established artists' guild, they will thrive under our sponsorship and illuminate our city to new glory.

As the free communes transitioned into Signorie (Lordships), the Ferrarese court became a center of Late Medieval chivalry. This was a cultural synthesis of French Arthurian legends and Italian humanist wit. It created a sophisticated courtly etiquette that has become the gold standard for European nobility, turning our court into a diplomatic hub where the 'Art of the Possible' is practiced through refined conversation and artistic patronage.

The University of Ferrara, founded by the Este and among the first of its kind, has attracted humanists and jurists from across Italy to our court. Under the guidance of eminent scholars, our classrooms become workshops of the New Learning, training the lettered servants and diplomats our growing state requires. This institution ensures that knowledge and new institutions spread faster through our lands than in any realm that relies on war alone.

Ferrara has originated the concept of the 'Ideal City'. Instead of organic medieval growth, the state will implement large-scale, planned urban expansions with wide boulevards and symmetrical plazas. This will be the first example of modern urban planning in Europe, designed to reflect the order and majesty of the state. It will improve public health, facilitate military movement, and make Ferrara the most modern and prestigious nation in the West.

Our court has become the most celebrated literary gathering in Italy, where poets recite in the great halls and scholars debate philosophy in the gardens, their work supported as an instrument of statecraft as much as a private pleasure. Our name is synonymous with excellence in the vernacular tradition, attracting talents from every corner of the peninsula who compete for our favor and patronage. This reputation for culture deepens our artistic heritage and turns every great work produced here into an advertisement for the prestige of our state.

The silkworms of our lands and the skilled hands of our weavers have long produced cloth of exceptional quality, and we have turned this craft into one of the most reliable pillars of our economy. By regulating the trade and protecting our master artisans, we ensure that raw silk is processed into finished goods here rather than exported cheaply to competitors. This mastery of the cloth trade keeps our merchant guilds prosperous and ensures that every bolt produced here carries the prestige of our name to the markets of Europe.

The marshy delta of the Po has long been a wasteland of standing water and malarial fog on our doorstep. By organizing a systematic program of drainage and embankment, we transform these wetlands into productive farmland, adding to our tax base while reducing the disease burden on our border communities. This transformation of the landscape into something orderly and profitable is our approach to governance made visible — the state as engineer of the land itself.

Some may call us bellicose, but that is only because they fear our might. A well-trained standing army is essential for survival in this chaotic age. Our adversaries will soon learn to respect our hardened spirit.

We have expanded our borders not only by the sword, but through careful financial planning, which allowed us to purchase influence over desirable territories — or to buy them outright. With continued wise budget management, this economic trend should be sustainable.

As in the case of Brabant, Guelders has traditionally been divided into four quarters. This system of provinces arranged around a strong central city has proven to be an efficient way to govern our nation, and we should apply this system to new regions that join our realm in the future.

Our strategic position within the Empire makes us an attractive staging ground for other princes' armies whenever outside threats arise. However, hosting foreign troops hurts our finances. To prevent this costly burden, we must raise our own troops and put them into service of the Empire.

A land of sands and flooded terrain, the people of Holland have always looked at the sea as their natural second home, where bountiful resources and glorious adventures await those brave enough to pursue them.

As a maritime nation, our sailors are accustomed to naval combat, whether against members of rival nations or pirates attempting to plunder our trading vessels. In any case, our navy must be prepared to face any enemy at any time.
Our country is surrounded by the sea, so it is only natural that we would brave the roiling waves in search of trading ports and enriching goods to bring back.

While our people always enjoyed superior literacy rates at all levels of society, this advantage is becoming more apparent in the world taking shape before us. Only those with a limited understanding would not take advantage of and increase this edge.

Standard volley fire involved each rank delivering its volley in one go to maximize firepower. But we have developed a different system of firing by platoon, with the idea being that one part of the regiment would always be firing at the enemy while others reloaded and got ready for the next volley. This removed time between attacks that the enemy could use to recover or otherwise gain an advantage.

Our nation is blessed with a well-established hub of cities focused on trade, and adventurous sailors willing to bring riches from all over the world back home. These seafarers will be an excellent way for us to trade with other nations and make significant profits.

the Netherlands has historically been at the forefront of technological and cultural advancements. We must continue to patronize inventors, artists, and writers to maintain our edge over other nations.

Our borders are not well-defended by natural features, as is the case in some other nations. However, we have wit and wisdom in abundance, enough to construct the mightiest fortifications possible to deter our enemies and protect our families.

For too long, our nation has been unevenly governed by multiple Stadtholders across different provinces, with the most powerful acting as Primus inter Pares among their peers. It is time to make the position hereditary and concentrate authority in a single ruler.

ref.d: With the invention of the fluyte, the Dutch shipbuilding industry has exploded. Domestic and foreign orders are streaming in, and business is booming! Never before have so many Dutch ships sailed the seas, and never before have so many of our people been employed in building them.

adv.d: For well over a century the Casa Gonzaga has ruled Mantua not as conquerors but as lords whose claim rests on a compact of mutual benefit with their subjects — a legitimacy that no merely military power can purchase and that we have maintained by never treating the city as a resource to be extracted. We sustain this standing through three interlocking channels: the church patronage that binds our subjects through shared devotion, the formal dynastic titles that give our rule a legal foundation that rivals cannot challenge, and our deliberate respect for the commune traditions that Mantua's citizens still recognize as their inherited right. This triple foundation of faith, dynasty, and civic compact gives our state a legitimacy that is felt by every subject rather than merely proclaimed from above, and makes our rule more stable than any arrangement built on force alone.

Our court has become one of the great magnets of artistic talent in the peninsula — painters, sculptors, and architects arrive already knowing that Mantua rewards ambition and that the work produced here will reach the eyes of every prince who sends an envoy to our door. We formalize this tradition of patronage into a deliberate policy, maintaining stipends and workshops that keep multiple artists resident at once and ensuring that the work they produce reflects the standing we intend to project. This culture of Mecenatismo reduces the cost of maintaining artists and draws talent of the highest quality to settle permanently among us rather than passing through for a single commission.

We establish a formal studium in Mantua, drawing teachers of law, philosophy, and the arts from the great universities of the region and providing the sons of our burghers and minor nobility with an education that was previously available only to those wealthy enough to travel to Bologna or Padua. The institution links Mantua to the network of European learning that flows through the great schools, bringing the latest ideas in jurisprudence, theology, and natural philosophy into our city rather than letting them arrive years late through correspondence. This Studium Mantovano raises the literacy of our governing class and ensures that new ideas take root among us as quickly as they spread anywhere in Italy.

Federico II Gonzaga commissioned Giulio Romano to build a pleasure palace on an island at the edge of the city, and what emerged was the Palazzo Te, one of the most inventive buildings of the Renaissance — a work of architecture that quotes the classical tradition with such knowing wit that scholars have argued over its ironies ever since. The frescoed rooms, from the giants collapsing in painted ruin to the horses of Federico's stables rendered with life-size confidence, are the most daring decorative program in northern Italy. This extraordinary achievement deepens our cultural tradition and gives the works produced under our patronage a singular character that collectors and courts seek out above the more conventional output of our rivals.

When Claudio Monteverdi staged L'Orfeo in our Palazzo Ducale for the Accademia degli Invaghiti, he gave the world its first fully realized opera — a work in which voices, instruments, and drama were fused into a form that audiences immediately recognized as unlike anything they had heard before. Mantua was the city where this transformation happened, and its court was the institution that made it possible, providing Monteverdi with singers, players, and the sustained patronage without which neither the rehearsals nor the score could have materialized. This primacy in the birth of opera makes our court the acknowledged origin of Europe's most powerful new art form, and the artists trained in its shadow carry our reputation to every stage they subsequently inhabit.

The lowland plain that surrounds Mantua on three sides is among the most fertile land in Italy, and we have made systematic investment in its management the foundation of our domestic economy — draining marshes, expanding irrigation channels, and regulating the reclamation of new land at the margins of the lakes that define our geography. The result is an agricultural capacity that grows reliably each generation, supplying our city with food surpluses that sustain a population larger than our politics alone would justify. This patient cultivation of the Pianüra Padâna (Pianura Padana in standard Italian: the Po Plain) ensures that our subjects eat well in difficult years and that our treasury collects the taxes of a prosperous countryside.

c.t: Is or was the country Byzantium (BYZ)

adv.d: We inherit some of the bureaucracy of our former empire, allowing us to maintain order and governance despite our reduced circumstances.
Let nobody forget that we are the descendants of the Komnenos that ruled over the Byzantine Empire. Although we now rule a different state, the legacy and prestige of our dynasty remains undeniable.

Our land is like our home; its forests, our garden. We know every bit of it better than anyone. Every path and every trail that crosses it is known to us, and we will make use of that knowledge if any dare to invade us.

The Komnenos dynasty may have been expelled from the Byzantine throne long ago, but its glory never faded. Members of our lineage are still shown the appropriate deference, and this respect and admiration stretches far beyond our borders.

Much as the Alps separate the French and Italian, the Pontic Mountains separate our last Greek holdout in Anatolia from the Turkic invaders who have seized the Anatolian Plateau. Pontus has always been more Greek than the rest of Anatolia; perhaps the legacy of the great Mithridates will inspire our warriors and strike as much fear into the Turks as he did the Romans?

The Laz have inhabited these lands for centuries. While our Empire was forged by Greek people, many Laz nonetheless remain within our borders. This has led to some of our enemies calling us Princes of the Laz in mockery, regarding us as inferiors. However, no matter what they say, it does not diminish our heritage, and we shall wear the title proudly.

Kingdoms are conquered not only by the sword. By forging marriage alliances with surrounding nations, we create opportunities to inherit their thrones — and, at the very least, extend stronger influence over them.

The great Byzantine Empire, under the rule of our forefathers, was truly something to behold. Deceit and treachery may have toppled their regime, but Byzantium has risen like the phoenix to reclaim its former glory, and now no one shall doubt our authority!

Since ancient times, Greek has been the language of education and science. When our ancestors came here, they not only brought their determination, but also their culture and native tongue. As such, the Greek tradition of learning is very much alive in our country.

Some remarkable women have emerged from along the Komnenos, and many among the rulers of Europe and even the infidels have sought their hands in matrimony. Our line is well-respected, and our princesses doubly so, for they are what allow foreign countries to claim legitimacy through our line, and us to maintain influence in foreign courts.
It is our faith that saves the souls of our people, and our clergy are the ones who ensure their salvation. What, then, are our monasteries, if not the source and origin of such salvation?

Isaakios Angelos, who deposed our line centuries ago, was himself deposed and blinded. On the pretense of putting the blind old fool back on the throne, the Venetian troops then sacked Constantinople. If there is something to learn from this incident, it is that treason and deceit are ubiquitous in the struggle for power, but they can also safeguard victory.

Even when it was called Trapezous in the mists of antiquity, our nation was the point where the land route across Asia meets the sea route leading to the Mediterranean. We grew famous as the terminal point for the great Silk Road, the wealth of China and India passing through our lands on its way to Europe. Since our nation still lies in this crucial location, there is no reason for us not to continue and encourage this steady flow of intercontinental trade.

Banished from our country, and yet our line survived. Forced to live in a mountainous wasteland surrounded by enemies, and yet our people thrived. We are a resourceful people, determined to make the most of what we have and to best whatever situation we encounter.

The Gesellschaft mit dem Fürspang is an order of knights formed to defend their interests and provide assistance to those who sponsor them. Providing them with extensive funds will grant us significantly more political prowess within our region and within the Holy Roman Empire.

The Roman aqueduct of Capsa, built in the second century to feed the legionary garrison and the surrounding olive estates from the springs of the Jebel Orbata, still channels water into our oasis through the same stone conduits that the Romans laid, maintained across the millennium by the resident communities of the ksar. Our hammam-baths, our orchard cisterns, and our market troughs all draw from this single inherited engineering, and our masons preserve the techniques required to patch and clean the conduit when sections collapse. This Roman-era hydraulic infrastructure gives Gafsa an oasis-throughput that no purely-medieval engineering could replicate from scratch.

The pomegranate orchards of Gafsa, famed across the Maghreb since the days of Ibn Khaldūn for their size, sweetness, and keeping qualities, and the date palms of our oasis belt produce fruits that the caravan-buyers of Tunis, Tripoli, and Sijilmasa specifically commission rather than accept substitutes. Our orchard owners hold hereditary leases on individual palm-and-pomegranate plots, our irrigation guildsmen apportion well-water by ancient share-table, and our caravan-masters price each consignment by origin grove rather than by bulk. This fruit-export specialization gives our oasis a niche-luxury revenue stream that no broader fruit-producing oasis can displace from the elite markets of the Mediterranean.

Our oasis sits at the Mediterranean-end of the western Saharan corridor. Caravans from Touat, Tafilalt, and the central Sahara converge on Gafsa before continuing north to the Sahel coast or east to the Hafsid heartland, while our merchant-houses provision the southbound legs with grain, cloth, and pottery. Our caravanserais host sub-Saharan, Berber, and Andalusi traders side by side; our customs officers tax the through-traffic at modest rates that keep the corridor profitable; and our oasis economy depends on the seasonal arrivals as much as on the resident orchards. This transit-polity role gives Gafsa a merchant-capacity and a diplomatic reach that no purely-agricultural oasis could sustain.

Our oasis preserves a distinct Berber substratum: the Gafsa-dialect, the matrilineal inheritance customs of the older clans, the pre-Islamic burial sites scattered across the Jebel Orbata, and the genealogies that trace many notable families back to the Zenata tribes of the pre-Hilāli era. Our Arabic and Berber speakers coexist in the same households, our judicial customary law preserves Berber tribal-precedent alongside the Mālikī shari'a, and our oral traditions preserve the Capsian and pre-Roman cultural memories that no Arabic-only southern oasis can claim. This dual cultural inheritance gives our urban culture a hybrid identity that the more thoroughly Arabized Sahel coastal towns cannot supply.

Our inter-tribal majlis, convening representatives of the Hammama, the Frashich, the Awlad Bouyahia, and the resident urban notables, meets quarterly in the central qasba to apportion irrigation rights, mediate caravan-route disputes, and ratify the local-share of tribute owed to whichever northern power claims us this generation. The chamber is hereditary but consultative, our notables serve without salary but accept hospitality and customary gifts, and our resolutions bind the participating tribes through customary law rather than imposed force. This institutionalized inter-tribal council gives our frontier oasis a political continuity that no purely-tribal or purely-urban government could sustain in our exposed position.

Our generation of reformist intellectuals, Gafsa-born and Zaytuna-trained, contributes correspondents, essayists, and modernist jurists to the Tunisian Nahḍa circles in the capital, balancing the metropolitan voices with the perspective of the southern oasis interior. Our pamphleteers debate beylical fiscal policy in the new Arabic press, our jurist-scholars publish commentaries on Khayr ad-Dīn's reform regulations, and our young administrators staff the new bureaus that the Sadiki graduates open in Tunis. This southern-intellectual presence gives our oasis a reformist-modernizing voice that no purely-metropolitan reform movement could otherwise capture from the frontier.

Our beloved city has been described as 'Diadema Regni', the Crown of the Empire, a moniker we strive mightily to maintain. Maintaining this distinction will help us remain above other Imperial cities in terms of our prestige and political influence.

b: Possible Burghers in Towns and Cities: +0.1
adv.d: The citizens of Mainz have prospered under the extensive rights granted to them by Adalbert of Mainz in the early 12th century. These rights, carved into the bronze door of the Cathedral, will serve as a reminder of cooperation between the separate powers within the city, both the clergy and the citizenry.

The Klüppelgesellschaft has been founded by a group of knights concerned about the erosion of our power within the Holy Roman Empire. It would be wise of us to sponsor those willing to fight for our status.

Our country's religious unity must be defended against any threat. If we provide our armies with moral guidance in the form of military chaplains, they will be much more motivated to defend our beliefs.

When the Rheinish League was active, we naturally assumed a position of leadership and guidance for the other members. Although the League itself has disbanded, we must do everything we can to maintain our influence over our former associates.

To ensure our lands are governed reliably, even in the absence of our ruler, we should instate a vicar. Empowered with extensive rights, the vicar can rule with our best intentions and remind the common folk of our presence at all times.

While celebrations on Ash Wednesday are a common occurrence, they hold especially deep roots in our country. While the public celebrates the Fastnacht, or carnival, with masquerade and excessive feasts, our court will engage in a special event. During the carnival celebrations, we will redistribute the roles of our court per lottery, with even the ruler having to participate. This custom of swapping roles, called Mainzer Königreich, will spread far beyond our borders and help expand our cultural legacy.
By expanding our already-growing printing industry, we can become the leading producer of books in Europe.

Defending our borders can be a difficult task, especially considering the river splitting our land in two. We must build an extensive network of garrisons and fortifications that can withstand our enemies.

Our sailors are used to navigating far and wide upon the seas, but control of the gulf surrounding us is what allows such travels. We must always stand ready to defend our waters against any foreign threat.

Our nation is at the back of the ample and hostile deserts of Arabia, but the sea to our east allows us to circumvent them. It is by sea, not by land, that we will need to perform our diplomacy, trade, and expansion.

Theoretically a merchant can be a citizen of the world, sailing to and from whichever port he pleases. We are going to give advantages to home merchants, for example, priority for loading and unloading of cargo, to ensure that our merchants have every incentive to bring their products home.
There are those who feel that we should not associate with unbelievers at all. We have done much to quash this, as only through association with heathen nations will we be able to trade with them.

To reap the full financial potential from trade, we need ships and any cargo they carry to be safe when docked in our ports. We must ensure that any areas that merchants consort in are free from petty crime.

As long as ships have been built in Arabia, there have been guilds who control the production. Although they may have performed a valuable service in keeping shipbuilding traditions alive, they now stand in the way of progress. We must open up the shipbuilding industry to all with talent.
We must ensure that our captains meet the highest standards of seamanship and nautical knowledge, ensuring that they will be able to use every advantage in all situations.
We must ensure that our merchants are always welcome wherever they go. Thus, we will use any means possible to make sure that all rulers we know about welcome our merchants.

Despite not being an island, our land is factually isolated from the rest of Arabia due to the surrounding deserts. As such, we have learned how crucial it is to have access to the sea, and how useful it will be for us if we take that option away from our enemies.

The Gesellschaft mit dem Fürspang is an order of knights formed to defend their interests and provide assistance to those who sponsor them. Providing them with extensive funds will grant us significantly more political prowess within our region and within the Holy Roman Empire.

After being hired and then betrayed by the Byzantine emperor, the ferocious Catalan Grand Company turned against their former paymasters and, in 1311, annihilated the Frankish duke Walter V of Brienne at the Battle of the Cephissus, seizing control of the Duchy of Athens and establishing a period of Catalan rule. These battle-hardened Almogàvers introduced a more ruthless mercenary ethos to Greek affairs, fortifying key strongholds, extracting tribute from the countryside, and maintaining their grip through a combination of terror and disciplined infantry tactics until internal strife and Aragonese intervention eventually shifted power back toward a more conventional feudal regime.

The workshops of Thebes, already renowned in Byzantine times for their silk-weaving, have flourished anew under Frankish rule as the dukes of Athens encourage Italian merchants to invest in looms, dyeworks, and export networks that carry Theban samites and velvets to markets from Bruges to Alexandria. This revival of luxury textile production, combined with the fertile plains of Boeotia that supply raw materials, generate substantial wealth that funds castle-building, knightly retinues, and the lavish lifestyle of the Athenian court, ensuring that the duchy remains one of the richest and most economically sophisticated territories of the entire Frankokratia.

Otto de la Roche, first Duke of Athens, established his court amid the ruins of the Acropolis, converting the ancient Parthenon into a Catholic cathedral dedicated to Our Lady while ruling over a duchy that stretched from Attica to Boeotia. Under his successors, the duchy became a surprising center of cultural exchange where Frankish knights patronized Greek scribes, Italian merchants traded in Piraeus, and scholars debated philosophy in sight of marble temples. All this produced a distinctive aristocratic society that prized both the martial virtues of chivalry and an appreciation for the Hellenic past that had so long been ignored by Western conquerors. We must reinstate this court to its past glory.

Modeled after the Venetian Arsenal but utilizing modern assembly-line techniques, our new dockyards at Piraeus can produce a fully equipped war galley in a matter of weeks. This industrialization of naval warfare allows the small Duchy to punch far above its weight class, maintaining a professional navy that dominates the Saronic Gulf. The Piraeus is no longer a ruin, but the most modern naval base in the Eastern Mediterranean.

As our rulers transitioned toward absolute rule, they replaced the fractious feudal lords with a meritocratic civil service drawn from the urban bourgeoisie. This centralized administration ensures that taxes are collected efficiently and the ruler's law is enforced uniformly from Marathon to Megara. By breaking the power of the old baronial families, our nation has become a streamlined, modern state capable of rapid mobilization.

Our artillery is now the finest in the world, benefiting from the metallurgical secrets of the world's renowned master-smiths and the chemical innovations of our local alchemists. The 'Thunder of Athens' is heard across the Balkans, as our cannons are prized for their range and reliability.

ref.d: Since the seizure of the Athens, the Catalan Company has projected considerable military influence over Greece.
