adv.d: Our rulers have always been skillful with their words, and their diplomatic acumen has established their influence far beyond our national borders. As time goes on and geopolitical pressures intensify, we must start cultivating friendship with other nations for protection while expanding our sphere of influence.

As a border province of the Holy Roman Empire, Hainaut has developed a rough-and-ready spirit, born from centuries of frontier conflict. This spirit makes our people naturally inclined towards taking defensive action, which we can exploit to our benefit.
Our lively urban settlements are full of potential. With just a little effort, we can make them and their hinterlands incredibly wealthy, allowing us to thoroughly tax them.

For centuries, mining has shaped our landscape, economy, and culture. Significant Silver discoveries in the region have attracted miners and traders from diverse regions, fostering the Ore Mountains' growth and expanding our realm's significance and development.

The Meißen Lion, also known as the Markmeißnische Löwe, holds a special place in heraldry. Representing the Wettin dynasty's symbol of power, an armored black lion with a red tongue gazes to the left on a golden field. Its image appears in various forms, including on painted tombstones, ensigns, helmets, coins, and seals, symbolizing the affiliation of the city of Meissen to the Mark Meißen and adorning the coats of arms of numerous towns and communities. Some link it to the recolored Thuringian lion.

Our people are truly resilient, embodying unwavering determination in the face of challenges. They weather adversity with unwavering spirit, finding strength in unity and a steadfast commitment to their shared values. Their indomitable resilience propels us forward, enabling us to overcome any obstacle that comes our way. We will always emerge stronger and more determined than ever before.

The Meißner groschen will serve as our national currency. This coin is based on the Prague groschen, which we will replace. This new large groschen will mark the beginning of a new era in the history of our coinage and will let us better control its influxes.

Religious infighting and intolerance plagues other lands, but we stand firm against allowing such strife to fester in our realm. Regardless of the diverse faiths our subjects hold, this nation shall be built on the strong pillars of tolerance and brotherhood, fostering a harmonious coexistence among all communities. United by a common vision, we will be forging a nation where respect and understanding flourish, paving the way for a prosperous future.

The Saxon Court is a pillar of Electoral Saxony's government, alongside civil and military administration. Court regulations define the responsibilities and daily routines of officials, while the court itself is composed of both nobles and peasants serving the ruling family in governance and administration. Traditionally, each adult member of the ruling family maintained their own household court, but we will now create a single, permanent court in our capital, attracting the finest minds in the realm.

Our valiant armies never waver! They demonstrate exceptional morale and loyalty, standing firm whether defending our realm or supporting allies. With indomitable spirits, they will press forward even in desperate circumstances, refusing defeat until physically unable to continue.

As the Reformation takes hold and the state assumes control over religious administration, a new responsibility arises for the emerging state: education, which was previously the duty of the Church. We will found princely schools at Pforta, Grimma, and Meissen using former monastic properties. Thus, the state will take on a significant role in shaping the educational landscape, fostering knowledge and intellectual growth for the future leaders of Saxony.
Saxony is the first country in Europe to produce Porcelain, which will bring wealth and prestige to the Wettin court.

Dresden and Leipzig, among other locales, have gained international recognition for being centers of Saxon Baroque culture. Magnificent architecture, like the Dresdner Hof, epitomize the grandeur of Saxony, while Johann Sebastian Bach's work has transformed Leipzig into a city of music and thriving highbrow culture. The region boasts unique expressions of culture, including handicrafts from the Ore Mountains and culinary traditions like the Dresdner Christstollen.

After tumultuous wars, a new era dawns upon Saxony — the remarkable Saxon Rétablissement. Amidst the ruins of our past, our nation will rise like a phoenix, rebuilding its shattered economy and charting a path toward prosperity. Driven by a blend of visionary state reforms and disciplined spending, our nation will emerge as a commercial hub. With unparalleled administrative prowess and a strategic focus on economic growth, this resolute transformation will mark a pivotal moment in history, shaping the destiny of Saxony well into the future.

Saxony's successful early industrialization is evident, with a highly developed industrial sector compared to other regions. The manufactory system, producing mainly for export, has flourished and will make Saxony a leading state in Germany's industrialization process. The emergence of smaller commercial landscapes and trade will be instrumental in promoting the region's economic growth and connections to other markets in Europe.

Since 1252, the gold Fiorino d'Oro struck at our mint has been the most trusted currency in Christendom, accepted without question from the counting houses of London to the bazaars of Alexandria because its weight and purity never varied through the ambitions of a dozen kings. Merchants who trade in florins trade in our reputation — every exchange carried out in our coin is a quiet advertisement for the solidity of Florentine governance and the reliability of the institutions that stand behind it. This universal confidence in our currency smooths every transaction conducted in our courts, and keeps the treasury supplied with the tax revenue that only a genuinely trusted medium of exchange can consistently generate.

The workshops of Florence — Giotto, Brunelleschi, Masaccio, Botticelli, and Leonardo — have redefined what painting and sculpture mean to an entire civilization, each generation expanding the boundaries of what the human eye and human hand can achieve in stone, pigment, and bronze. No patron who wishes to be taken seriously commissions a work without first consulting Florentine masters, and our artists carry this reputation wherever they are summoned, turning the name of the city into a credential that outlasts any individual canvas. This unbroken tradition of artistic leadership fills our ateliers with the finest talent in Italy and ensures that the works we produce command the admiration — and the gold — of the most demanding patrons in Christendom.

Machiavelli's argument against mercenary armies fell for generations on reluctant ears — the guilds preferred to pay condottieri than to march themselves — but the catastrophes of 1494 and 1512 demonstrated at ruinous cost what hired soldiers will and will not die for. We answer by organizing the men of our districts into standing companies, trained and equipped at public expense, whose stake in the defense of Florence is not a monthly wage but their own homes and trades. This commitment to arming our own citizens produces infantry that will hold when paid soldiers would retreat, giving our army a core of men who fight for something that cannot be renegotiated at the end of the campaign season.

The military engineers of our city have mastered the design of low-profile angled bastions whose sloped walls scatter artillery fire and eliminate the blind spots that made older round towers so easy to undermine. Every significant stronghold we build draws on the geometry our architects have refined, producing fortifications that are both cheaper to garrison and far harder for any attacker to breach. This mastery of the Trace Italienne makes our walls the most modern in Italy and transforms the cost of holding them into a manageable advantage rather than a treasury drain.

In the house of Count Giovanni de' Bardi, musicians, poets, and scholars have been gathering to recapture what they imagine the performance style of ancient Greek tragedy must have sounded like — a quest that will produce something entirely new and entirely ours. The conversations, experiments, and compositions that emerge from these evenings are drawing gifted performers who value the creative freedom our court offers over the higher wages they might command elsewhere. This circle of artistic innovators, the Camerata Fiorentina, makes our city the origin of a musical revolution that will spread our influence into every court that hears what we have created.

The great families of our city have built commercial networks that span the continent — agents in London, factors in Bruges, correspondents in Alexandria — so that the letters of exchange bearing our names pass as freely as coin in cities that have never seen our walls. By formalizing and expanding these networks under the protection of our constitutional government, we ensure that our merchants operate from a position of stability and trust that no prince-led rival can easily replicate. This reach of our Merchant Houses drives the revenue of every trade we conduct and opens the most distant and profitable markets to the goods our workshops produce.
We have been granted the rulership of Bavaria directly by the Emperor! By embellishing ourselves as the divinely-appointed protectors of Bavaria, we will ensure our legitimacy cannot be questioned.

Our nobles have distinguished themselves as formidable knights in the service of the Holy Roman Empire. We should nurture and scrupulously maintain these troops to ensure the survival of our ducal integrity.
Our lands are rich in the crops and fresh water required to brew beer, and our people readily enjoy this abundance. Many small breweries could grow into successful businesses, with the right support.

Our lands are frequently crossed by merchants wishing to trade Salt, Silver, and Livestock in the rich lands to our south. We would be foolish not to take advantage of their presence, and therefore will establish bustling trade hubs in our own lands to attract their business.

With our homeland at the feet of the beautiful Alps, we are a destination for artists from all over Europe, who seek inspiration in our incredible landscape. If we were to construct and support the appropriate cultural institutions, we could refine our court into a center of refinement and elegance, one that could rival even the most prestigious powers of Europe.
We once were ruled by Bavaria, unified in culture and allied under a single banner. We must ensure that the new Bavarian state is equally mighty, a home worthy of its strong and proud people.
Establishing a council with the sole duty of advising our ruler during times of conflict will help us develop a more capable fighting force.
We must ensure our people remain united in their faith, and that they will not be divided by heretical thoughts.
Only with a formidable standing army will we have the military might necessary to match our ambitions. With careful focus, we can expand it without having a ruinous impact on our state's finances.

No matter if we are answering to an Imperial overlord or cozying up to a potential foreign ally, our diplomats must be prepared for everything. But only if they keep Bavarian interests first and foremost in their efforts will we be able to claim true success in our diplomatic maneuverings.
Our realm needs a new standardized coin to serve as our national unified currency. Establishing a state-owned mint in our capital would ensure our total control over this new coinage.

The excellent quality of our beer has been celebrated for centuries, but for our brews to achieve legendary status, we must ensure their continued prestige and superiority for all time. Several rulers in the past have created regulations and standards for the brewing of this wonderful substance; and we could use this fact as a stamp of our breweries' quality.

The triarchs of Negroponte divided the lordship of the long island among three families, yet managed to maintain a unified naval policy that dominates the narrow Euripos channel and extracts tolls from every vessel passing between the Aegean and the northern ports. Their galleys, crewed by a mixture of Frankish knights, Greek mariners, and Italian mercenaries, patrol the straits with ruthless efficiency, ensuring that Negroponte remains one of the wealthiest and most strategically vital outposts of the Frankokratia.

The island of Euboea is divided among three Terzieri, or Triarchs, creating a competitive yet unified defensive structure that prevents any single lord from becoming weak. This tripartite system ensures that if one fortress falls, the other two mobilize instantly, creating a redundant and resilient military administration. This internal rivalry keeps our garrisons at peak readiness, as no Triarch wishes to be outdone by his peers.

The narrow channel separating our island from the mainland is the most strategic chokepoint in Central Greece, controlled by our massive swing-bridge and fortified towers. By taxing the flow of goods between Boeotia and the Aegean, we have transformed a geographic oddity into a permanent source of toll revenue. We hold the key to the movement of armies in the Balkans, and we charge a heavy price for its use.

The unique, reversing tides of the Euripus Strait have been harnessed by our engineers to power a series of massive tidal mills. These machines provide consistent energy for milling grain, sawing ship-timber, and powering forge-bellows regardless of the wind. This technological advantage makes Euboea the most industrially advanced island in the Mediterranean, capable of out-producing its maritime rivals.

To ensure the quality of our fleet, the three lords of the island have co-founded an academy for the training of naval officers and navigators. Students are taught the latest in astronomical navigation and maritime law, ensuring that every Euboean captain is a professional of the highest caliber. This focus on naval education keeps our fleet at the cutting edge of maritime warfare and exploration.

Using the high-quality silica sands of our beaches and the soda ash from our coastal plants, we have established a glass-making industry that rivals Murano. Our mirrors and stained glass are exported to the great palaces of the Latin Empire and the West, bringing immense wealth to the island. This luxury industry provides the tax revenue needed to maintain our massive coastal walls in an age of gunpowder.

The art of painting has flourished in Italy since the beginning of the Renaissance, but no artists can match the elegance of those trained in Siena, where the Studium Senese — one of the oldest universities in Europe — ensures that painters and scholars alike are nurtured by the same tradition of civic patronage. Sienese art is otherworldly and refined, with a heavy focus on the miracles performed by Biblical figures and Saints. This unity of learning and artistry defines the Sienese school, securing its reputation for centuries to come.

The Nine Priors of our republic — drawn exclusively from the merchant guilds of Siena and barred to the high nobility whose factional rivalries brought every previous government to ruin — have shaped the city's governance with an administrative diligence that our more aristocratic neighbors cannot match. Their terms are brief and their accountability public, making sustained corruption harder to conceal and factional manipulation harder to dress in the language of civic virtue. This tradition of merchant governance gives our institutions a practical competence and a legitimacy grounded in commerce and consent rather than an accident of birth.

Our magistrates have established the Monte dei Paschi — a public lending institution secured against the revenues of the Maremma pastures — to provide affordable credit to merchants and the poor alike and to give Siena a stable foundation for commerce in an era of expanding trade. This innovation in public finance became a model of banking stability that outlasted empires, sustaining our commercial life through crises that bankrupted more reckless rivals. This institution accelerates the adoption of new economic practices across our lands while generating the steady fiscal revenue that a city of ambition requires.

Caterina di Giacomo di Benincasa — mystic, theologian, and doctor of the faith — remains the most celebrated soul that Siena has ever produced, and in the age of religious upheaval that followed the great disputes of the era her memory became a rallying point for a confident, devotional faith that answered challenge with piety rather than polemic. Sienese scholars and preachers placed themselves at the forefront of this spiritual renewal, drawing on the saint's writings to argue that reform must begin in the heart before it reaches the law. This legacy of sanctity and conviction deepens the faith of our people and draws together communities that might otherwise fracture under the pressures of religious conflict.

Twice each year the contrade of Siena compete in the Palio — a bareback horse race around the Piazza del Campo that is as much a civic ritual as a contest, binding the neighborhoods of the city in a shared drama of rivalry, identity, and fierce communal pride. The elaborate pageantry of the event draws visitors from across Italy and broadcasts Sienese cultural vitality to all who witness it, reinforcing our reputation as a city that has not forgotten how to celebrate itself. This enduring tradition amplifies our influence across the region and wins us the admiration of courts that see in Siena a living testament to the power of civic culture.

Even as the grand ambitions of the Sienese republic gave way to foreign pressure and Tuscan consolidation, the citizens of Siena maintained a fierce pride in their distinct identity — their dialect, their art, their tradition of communal self-governance — that made the city difficult to absorb without provocation. Those who sought to antagonize or diminish Siena found its people stubborn in their resistance, bound together by centuries of shared memory and an insistence that Sienese life meant something worth defending. This deep-rooted civic spirit discourages aggression against us and sustains the prosperity that flows from a population genuinely invested in the wellbeing of the city they call home.

Our territory is both home to many urban areas and castles of many imperial knights. Balancing them and their often opposing interests is no easy task. Only if they cooperate with us and the cathedral chapter, we can ensure the functionality of our government.

Because Argos is the most neutral and secure port in the Peloponnese, it has become the preferred meeting ground for the ambassadors of the Latin states. We have established a permanent 'Diplomatic Quarter' where treaties are negotiated and alliances are forged between the Frankish lords and the Great Powers. This role as a regional mediator grants us an international influence that protects us from being annexed by our larger neighbors.

As the House of Brienne maintains claims to Jerusalem and Cyprus, Argos has become a center for 'Chivalric Genealogy'. Knights from across the West come here to prove their lineage or seek titles in the 'crusader fringe'. This constant influx of high-born adventurers provides a rotating pool of talented officers for our local levies.

The Palamidi fortress, perched high above the Gulf of Argos, has been expanded into a complex system of seven interlocking forts that command the entire Argolid. By controlling this 'Gibraltar', we dictate the movement of any fleet attempting to supply an army in the Morea, effectively making the lordship unconquerable by land or sea. This strategic dominance allows us to play the role of kingmaker between our neighbors.

Recognizing that the future of warfare is determined by the cannon, we have turned our high-altitude forts into laboratories for ballistics and gunnery. Our officers are trained to calculate firing arcs from extreme heights, allowing our batteries to hit enemy ships with pinpoint accuracy. The Argos School of Gunnery is respected across Europe for its mathematical precision and tactical innovation.

Capitalizing on our position as a safe harbor, the merchant houses of Nauplia have developed a sophisticated system of maritime insurance and risk-sharing for Aegean trade. By guaranteeing the safety of Latin cargoes against piracy and storms, we have turned our port into the financial safe haven of the Peloponnese. This early form of financial capitalism draws capital away from the larger Italian republics and concentrates it in our own local banks.

adv.n: The Curia of the Two Benches
adv.d: In a daring move toward social stability, the Lordship has reformed the high court of Nauplia into the Curia of the Two Benches. This judicial body requires that every civil case involving land or inheritance be heard by a panel consisting of one Frankish judge and one Greek Demogeron (Elder). By institutionalizing this 'Shared Justice', we have effectively ended the centuries-old legal friction between the Latin and Orthodox populations. This governance model has created a unique 'Argive Identity' that is fiercely loyal to the Lordship, protecting the state from the revolutionary fervors sweeping through the rest of Europe.

ref.d: Since the seizure of the Athens, the Catalan Company has projected considerable military influence over Greece.
