u.t: Chivalric order: Order of Saint Hubert

adv.d: The Hubertusorden will serve as a glorious reminder of our knights' combat prowess! Joining the order will be a reward for our loyal knights, and its members will display our glory for all to see.

The five fortified Ibadi cities of the M'zab valley (Ghardaïa, Beni Isguen, Bou Noura, Melika, and El Atteuf) rise above the Wādī M'zab as a refuge for the Ibadi survivors of the Rustamid kingdom destroyed at Tāhart in 909. Each city is built as a fortified qṣar with its mosque-tower serving as both minaret and watchtower, governed by the consensus of its founding-families and bound to its sisters by intermarriage and a shared halqa al-'azzāba religious council. This pentapolitan foundation gives our Ibadi community a fortified-urban heritage no other Saharan settlement can match.

Our communities practice the doctrine of taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation) when interacting with Sunni-majority neighbors, professing common Sunni forms in public while maintaining strict Ibadi orthodoxy within the pentapolis walls. Our women are veiled and confined to the home courtyards, our markets segregate visitors from the inner sacred spaces, and our jurists publicly defer to the Mālikī fatwās of Algiers and Tunis while privately following their own al-Madhhab al-Wahbī line. This doctrine of religious-cultural seclusion preserves our distinct Ibadi identity through centuries of Sunni political pressure that have erased every other Khārijī community.

Our scholars at Beni Isguen and Ghardaïa compile the great Ibadi-Wahbī jurisprudence — the Kitāb an-Nīl of Sheikh 'Abd al-'Azīz ath-Thamīnī, the legal commentaries of Atfayyash and Bābū — codifying centuries of fiqh al-'ibādiyya into a written reference corpus. We send our promising young students from each pentapolis-city to the others to learn from the senior 'azzāba councils, and our scholarly graduates serve as judges, scribes, and missionaries across the broader Ibadi world from Oman to Zanzibar. This codification gives our religious establishment a depth and coherence that no Sunni-Maghrebi madrasa tradition can match within our own sect.

The first Mozabite merchant families (the Bayyūḍs, the Atfayyashes, the Bā Ḥaqqs) begin establishing trading houses in Algiers, Constantine, Tunis, and the smaller Algerian coastal towns, sending their sons north to learn commerce while their daughters remain at home in the pentapolis. Our diaspora merchants serve as a financial-information network for the Ibadi community at home, extending Ibadi credit, sourcing grain in lean years, and channeling profits back into pentapolis endowments. This emerging diaspora gives our state a financial reach across the Maghreb that no Saharan community of comparable size has ever achieved.

Each Mzab city is governed by its own djemaa (an assembly of family-head representatives) which meets in the city mosque-courtyard to debate civic affairs, settle disputes, and elect the council of 'azzāba who exercise ultimate moral authority. The djemaa system has no inherited offices or noble privileges; every adult male of the founding-families holds an equal vote, and the assembly's collective rulings bind even the wealthiest merchant houses. This proto-republican consensus governance gives our pentapolis a political stability rooted in religious-communal solidarity that no autocratic sultanate can match.

Our late-nineteenth-century intellectuals (Sheikh Muḥammad ben Yūsuf Atfayyash, the Pole of the Wahbiyya; Sheikh Ibrāhīm Bayyūḍ; and the younger generation of Salafiyya reformers) open the Mzab to dialogue with the wider Islamic reformist movements of Cairo, Damascus, and the Indian Ocean. We send our students to Tunis and Cairo, our journals from Ghardaïa engage with the Salafi press of Algiers and Constantine, and our pentapolis scholarly tradition meets the wider Ibadi world of Zanzibar and Oman on equal footing. This modernist intellectual revival binds the scattered Ibadi world into a shared modern community that any centralizing foreign administration cannot easily fragment.
Our ancestors ruled the lands of Tamil Nadu for centuries. In these times when we are dominated by foreign invaders, we should rely on our ancient connections to this land to justify our rule.

Our troubled history records both victories and crushing defeats. If we want to endure and dominate as a significant power once more, we must develop a thorough understanding of how to best utilize our native terrain to delay and stall hostile armies until we can mount a direct resistance.

Throughout our turbulent history, we never wavered in the face of conflict and insurmountable odds. We need to weaponize this determination, and use it to instill a sense of fervor into our people that will inspire them to fight harder than ever.

Our people have developed an outstanding skill for diving for and harvesting pearls along our coasts. While this has clear economic benefits, the natural affinity our people have for water makes them excellent and easily-trained sailors, granting us an edge against our seafaring foes.

The lands of southern India have long endured the incursions of foreign invaders and upstart warlords looking to establish their own domains. We must use the grand history of our ancient dynasty to lay claim to this land, as only we can bring stability and peace back to our rightful territory.

For three centuries, Pisa stood among the dominant sea powers of the western Mediterranean, its galleys reaching every harbor from Sardinia to the Levant and its naval victories over the Saracens earning the city privileged access to markets that lesser powers could not enter. The defeat at Meloria in 1284 diminished our fleet, but could not erase what those centuries of seaborne commerce built — our captains know these waters, our traders know their counterparts in every port, and the routes that made us great are still routes that we can sail. This seafaring legacy gives our merchants an advantage in the Western trade sphere that no landlocked rival can replicate, and the memory of maritime greatness drives us to rebuild what was taken from us.

Founded in 1343 by imperial charter and rebuilt after each political upheaval that swept through Pisa, our university has trained jurists, physicians, and theologians whose careers carried the Pisan tradition of rigorous scholarship into the courts and churches of Italy and beyond. What distinguishes the Studio Pisano is not merely its age, but also its methods — the faculty has consistently attracted scholars who prefer questions to answers, building an institutional habit of inquiry that produces graduates capable of more than memorizing received doctrine. This tradition of active scholarship shapes the quality of every professional we train, raising the standard of learning across our institutions and ensuring that knowledge remains a living practice rather than a performed ceremony.

The quarries supplying Pisa and the surrounding coast have long produced some of the finest white marble in Italy, used in the great churches and civic monuments that define our skyline. Sculptors and architects trained in this tradition have become sought-after across the peninsula, and the stone itself commands high prices from patrons who wish to build in the Pisan manner. This mastery of stone raises our cultural standing and ensures that every contract signed and shipment sold carries with it the prestige of a city that knows how to make the world beautiful.

The scholars of Pisa have pursued understanding through careful observation and measurement rather than received authority alone, building on a long tradition of inquiry in our Studio Pisano that spans mechanics, astronomy, and the natural arts. This empirical habit of mind has shaped not only our philosophers but our engineers and commanders, who approach problems with the same rigor that our scholars apply to the motion of the heavens. This culture of natural philosophy disciplines our military thinking and gives our forces a tactical precision that more tradition-bound armies cannot match.

The medical faculty of the University of Pisa is anchored by the Orto Botanico — among the oldest university botanical gardens in the world — where students study the healing properties of plants and develop methods to treat epidemic disease more effectively. Physicians trained in Pisa carry this empirical tradition across the country, improving outcomes for the sick and reducing the toll that plague and pestilence exact on our population. This commitment to medical learning strengthens the resilience of our people and spreads the literacy that comes naturally to those trained in the careful arts of diagnosis and record-keeping.

Centuries of scholarly excellence have made the name of Pisa synonymous with learning and refined culture among the educated courts of Italy and beyond. Foreign students and wealthy patrons prize a Pisan education as a mark of distinction, and the artistic works produced in this atmosphere of cultured ambition command premium prices from discerning collectors who associate the city with quality. This reputation for scholarship elevates our standing in foreign courts and enriches those who produce and sell the works of art our academic tradition inspires.

The mountain lords of Salona, perched around the ancient site of Delphi and controlling the strategic passes into central Greece, maintain a fierce independence through a combination of rugged terrain, stout fortifications, and a martial tradition that draws fighting men from across the Frankokratia. Even as larger states collapse, the lords of Salona repeatedly defy their enemies, turning their highland fief into a safe refuge of Latin knighthood in Greece and a persistent irritant to every power that seeks to dominate the region between the Corinthian Gulf and the Spercheios valley.

Deep within the rugged mountains of our lordship lie veins of metals that have been forgotten since the days of the Delphic Oracle. By bringing in Saxon mining experts and applying Western smelting technology, we have turned the Mount of the Muses into a center of heavy industry. The wealth extracted from these mines allows the Lords of Salona to maintain a court that rivals the Dukes of Athens in elegance and power.

adv.n: The Asceticism of the Crissaean Crags
adv.d: The soil of Salona is a miserly host, offering little food besides mountain herbs to those who dwell in the shadow of the peaks. Life in this jagged landscape has bred a peasantry and knightly class alike who are famously indifferent to hunger and hardship. Our soldiers require half the rations of a Frankish man-at-arms, possessing a lean, wolf-like endurance that allows them to out-march and out-climb any adversary. In the high passes of Phocis, the belly is light, but the resolve is as unyielding as the mountain itself.

Wheeled transport is pretty much impossible in most of our domain; thus, we have established a state-run Chancery to nationalize the logistics of the mountains. This allows us to move supply trains at a pace that leaves conventional imperial armies starving in the crags.

In the shifting power dynamics, Salona has moved beyond simple feudal oaths to a predatory legal doctrine known as the 'Wolf-Pacts'. By legally defining our neighbors as 'client-prey' that require Salona's 'alpha' protection to survive, we create a permanent diplomatic justification for intervention and annexation. This predatory diplomacy allows us to absorb smaller lordships and border-fiefs under the guise of 'Defensive Consolidation', ensuring that the Latin presence in the Balkans is led by a single, sharp-toothed power rather than a scattered, vulnerable pack.

adv.n: The Legacy of the Alpha Protector
adv.d: The 'Wolf-Pacts' have reached their logical conclusion: the Hegemony is the recognized 'Alpha' of the Eastern Mediterranean. We no longer justify aggression. We simply exercise our natural mandate to 'police' the Levant. This projection of power ensures that the Greek seas remain a private lake for the merchants of Salona.

Bologna became the intellectual laboratory of Europe with the rise of its organized university, the oldest in the world, earning the nickname of La Dòta (La Dotta in standard Italian: the Learned). Culturally, this moved the society away from feudal trial-by-combat toward a civilian jurisprudence based on recovered Roman Law. This produced a class of professional lay-notaries and judges who could manage complex urban administrations, giving Bologna an unmatched bureaucratic efficiency.

Through the fertile bounty of the Po Valley and the mastery of the Bolognese guilds, our capital will earn a reputation for unparalleled opulence and a second nickname: La Grâsa (or La Grassa, the Fat One, in standard Italian). By investing in the Quadrilatero markets and the production of refined meats and pastas, we will ensure that every traveler leaves with a full stomach and a lighter purse.

La Råssa (the Red, or La Rossa in standard Italian), as Bologna is also known, celebrates the crimson soul of our skyline; the ancient terracotta brickwork and the defensive sea of red rooftops seen from the Asinelli Tower inspire awe in our subjects and defiance against our foes. Red is becoming so associated with our city that we must start creating laws to make sure that anything not currently in our preferred palette is rebuilt in red terracotta as soon as possible.

As the wild energy of the Renaissance cools, education is shifting toward organized Academies. These are state-sponsored institutions for scientists, writers, and painters, whose aim is to reform art education by moving away from Mannerism toward naturalism and life drawing. These reforms will allow the state to direct artistic and scientific production toward national prestige, leading to the birth of the 'Bolognese School' of painting, which will dominate European tastes for decades.

Bologna will become the center of development for the concerto and the professionalization of the orchestra. By abandoning the unpredictable modal traditions of the past, we will establish the rigid architectural laws of modern major-minor tonality. This synthesis will transform the violin from a folk instrument into the primary voice of the Baroque era, standardizing the Trio Sonata and the Concerto Grosso. This apparent simplicity will soon become the benchmark of prestige, spreading from Italian cathedrals to the most distant European courts. It will also represent the final transition from the experimental Renaissance to the era of disciplined, instrumental virtuosity.

The University of Bologna remains at the cutting edge of the Enlightenment. The discovery of animal electricity in a Bolognese laboratory has laid the groundwork for modern bio-electricity and physics. This spirit of inquiry will turn the city into a hub for early industrial and scientific pioneers, bridging the gap between ancient scholasticism and the modern laboratory.

u.t: Chivalric order: Order of Saint Hubert

adv.d: The Hubertusorden will serve as a glorious reminder of our knights' combat prowess! Joining the order will be a reward for our loyal knights, and its members will display our glory for all to see.

Liège has been a cultural center for centuries, the home of the most celebrated scholars in the region and the envy of our rivals. But we shall not allow ourselves to become complacent; we shall never stop improving our institutions.

As part of one of the biggest dioceses in the area, there is no doubt as to the depth of devotion our people hold. We will show the world that our faith in God is as strong as our faith in our nation.

Our nation inspires artists from across Europe, who come here to create their masterworks. We will spare no expense to support these artists and attract new talent, establishing ourselves as a hub of arts and culture.

We have long woven the finest Lucchese Silk Brocade in all of Italy, and our looms have made our city prosperous beyond its size. Our weavers' guilds protect the secrets of the craft and ensure the quality that commands high prices in distant markets. This mastery of cloth transforms raw threads into the foundation of our republic's wealth.

The great towers built by our noble families rise above the rooflines of our city, each one a declaration of prestige and power within the republic. The Torre Guinigi stands tallest among them, crowned with the ilex trees that have become the emblem of our city. These towers remind all who enter that our strength rests in the ambition and rivalry of citizens who have learned to compete in stone.

We have encircled our city with a great ring of Renaissance bastions, one of the finest defensive works of the age, completed over decades of labor and civic investment. The walls are so wide at the base that walkways run along their tops, and they have never been breached by any enemy. This fortification has allowed us to remain free where neighboring cities have fallen.

We have maintained our independence by navigating the religious upheavals of the age through careful and measured diplomacy. Our commitment to our faith has been sincere but never fanatical, allowing us to preserve the goodwill of both the devout and the pragmatic. This balance of piety and prudence has become the art by which our republic endures.

Our city has long nurtured the musical arts, drawing composers and performers to its churches, salons, and public celebrations. Our chapelmasters and instrument-makers have achieved such renown that talented Musicians seek appointment here as a mark of distinction. This tradition turns our city into a stage and fills its streets with an art we have made unmistakably our own.

Our ancient Republican Constitution has survived the ages through careful governance and the determination of our citizenry to resist tyranny. When neighboring cities fell to princes and conquerors, we maintained our written laws and our councils without interruption. This enduring order gives our state a stability that larger and more powerful neighbors cannot easily replicate.

The ancient blood of the Paleologue gives our marquisate a dignity and legitimacy that commands respect from the greatest courts of Europe. This lineage connects us to a world of ceremony and diplomacy that most smaller states can only admire from afar. We carry this heritage as a shield as much as an ornament, using it to open doors that our armies alone could never unlock.

We have made Casale Monferrato the heart of our state, a city that grows in commerce and craft under the shelter of our rule. The merchants and guilds of the city bring life to its streets and revenues to our treasury, and its position on the roads between great powers makes it a natural gathering place for trade. This city is our richest possession and the proof of what sound governance can build.

Our court has become a gathering place for artists, scholars, and musicians drawn by the patronage and refined taste we offer. We prize the Arts of the Court as instruments of prestige, and the works produced under our roof reflect well on our name wherever they travel. This investment in culture returns in reputation what it costs in coin.

We have transformed Casale Monferrato into a fortress city whose walls and bastions are among the most formidable in the peninsula. The citadel's deep ditches and angled walls are designed to exhaust any siege and bleed any attacker who thinks to take it quickly. This fortification has made our seat of power into one of the great military prizes of the age, too costly to assault and too important to ignore.

We have survived between greater powers through the arts of flexibility and careful friendship, never placing our trust entirely in any single alliance. By maintaining a reputation for reasonableness and good faith, we have made ourselves useful to those who might otherwise simply absorb us. This Diplomatic Resilience is our oldest strategy and our most reliable one.

The rolling hills and fertile valleys of our marquisate yield harvests that sustain our people and support a growing population of farmers and rural craftsmen. Through careful management and investment in our lands, we have expanded the reach of our agriculture into slopes and terraces that once lay idle. This Agricultural Transformation brings new settlers to our countryside and new revenues to our state.

Marco I Sanudo, a Venetian noble who participated in the Fourth Crusade, seized the Cyclades archipelago in 1207 and founded the Duchy of Naxos, creating a maritime feudal state whose lords ruled from fortified island citadels and drew income from trade, piracy suppression, and the fertile valleys of Naxos, Paros, and Santorini. By blending Venetian commercial instincts with Frankish feudal organization, the Sanudo dynasty has maintained a semi-independent duchy that serves as a vital link in the Latin trade network, protecting shipping lanes while extracting tolls and offering safe harbors to Crusader, Genoese, and Venetian vessels alike.

The scattered islands of the Aegean demand constant vigilance from their Latin rulers, who maintain fleets of light galleys to patrol against pirates, raiders, and rival Italian maritime powers. The dukes of Naxos and their vassals have developed a sophisticated system of island garrisons, signal fires, and swift courier vessels that allow them to respond rapidly to threats across the archipelago, while the wealth extracted from trade protection and harbor dues enables the construction of sturdy coastal fortresses that make the Cyclades one of the most secure regions of the Frankokratia, a maritime bulwark.

As the demand for fine art rises, the demand for high-quality Parian marble has returned to levels not seen since the days of Augustus. By reopening the ancient quarries and employing modern engineering techniques, we have turned a geologic quirk into a fountain of wealth that funds our Aegean hegemony. The palaces of Rome and Paris are increasingly built with stone hewn from our sovereign islands.

Our nobility is unique in the Western world; they are knights who have traded the horse for the galley and the lance for the boarding pike. These 'Sea-Knights' roam the Eastern Mediterranean under the Ducal banner, enforcing a 'Latin Peace'. This aggressive stance keeps our sailors sharp and our rivals' trade in constant peril.

In an era of global trade, our islands have become the indispensable waystations of the Mediterranean, providing fresh water, ship timber, and salted meats to long-haul vessels. By standardizing the port facilities across our twenty-odd islands, we ensure that any merchant ship must pay for the privilege of our hospitality. This logistics network makes us the undisputed masters of the Aegean's internal economy.

In an age of global exploration and precision, the Dukes of Naxos have established the premier center for Mediterranean cartography and maritime science. By employing the finest astronomers and clockmakers to map every reef, current, and wind pattern of the Cyclades, we have made our navigational charts the most sought-after tools in the world. This scientific mastery ensures that Naxiot captains can navigate the treacherous Aegean at night or in storm, granting our merchant and war fleets a decisive advantage in speed and safety over any foreign interloper.

The da Carrara family have governed Padua for over a century as lords whose authority rests on a combination of personal prestige, legal sanction from the empire, and a genuine investment in the prosperity of the city they rule. Our administration has maintained the civic institutions that the commune period established, channeling their energy into the service of seignorial government rather than displacing them, and the result is a city that functions with unusual smoothness. This tradition of Signoria that respects the civic fabric it inherits gives our urban governance an efficiency that reduces the cost of keeping our subjects settled and loyal.

Founded in 1222, the Bò — named for the inn where its first students gathered — has never ceased to be one of the great centers of European learning, and Padua's willingness to teach subjects that more cautious universities declined has made it a destination for the curious minds of every generation. Vesalius performed his anatomical demonstrations here, Galileo lectured from its chair of mathematics, and the law faculty has trained judges and administrators across the continent. This unbroken tradition of free inquiry raises the literacy and capacity of the burgher class that relies on the university and attracts scholars whose presence keeps the city's intellectual life in motion.

The medical faculty of Padua has been recognized across Europe as the most rigorous training ground for physicians since the university was founded, combining systematic anatomical study with clinical observation in a way that the great Arab compilations alone could never provide. The students who pass through its dissection theater carry an understanding of the body more detailed and more precise than any other school in the Christian world could offer, and the physicians they become have changed how illness is understood and treated in every city they subsequently serve. This tradition of empirical medicine gives our population a resistance to epidemic disease that more superstition-dependent approaches cannot produce and deepens the literacy of every educated class the university touches.

The philosophy faculty of Padua has developed a tradition of rational inquiry into the natural world that operates on Aristotelian premises while reaching conclusions that trouble the Church far more than open theology might have. In Padua, it is considered legitimate to argue that the soul is mortal, that intellect is collective rather than individual, and that natural causes could explain what elsewhere requires divine intervention. This culture of secular reasoning produces lawyers, physicians, and administrators of unusual intellectual independence, trained to analyze rather than simply to accept authority. The reputation of the Paduan School makes our state a gathering point for minds that produce more careful governance, and draw scholars who enrich our city's intellectual life.

We establish the Accademia Patavina di Scienze Lettere ed Arti to gather the leading scholars, physicians, and men of letters of the city into a single institution with the formal backing of the state — a structure that turns the individual brilliance of the university's faculty into a sustained collective enterprise capable of undertaking projects no single professor could manage. The Accademia provides a forum where the results of the university's research meet the practical needs of administration and commerce, making learned expertise available to the state at a fraction of the cost of maintaining separate advisory bodies. This institutionalization of scholarship gives our court an unusual depth of technical and administrative counsel and keeps talented men in our service who might otherwise seek the grander stages of larger states.

The oldest municipal institutions of our city — the elected councils, the written statutes, the tradition of citizen participation in public decisions — have never been fully extinguished, even through the decades of seignorial government that placed a single family above them. We revive and formalize these communal structures, giving our merchants and burghers a recognized role in civic governance and restoring the sense that the city belongs to all its citizens rather than its rulers alone. This Comùn Padovàn (Comune Padovano in standard Italian: Paduan Commune) channels the energy of our most active citizens into institutions that serve the state, increasing the tax revenue that flows from a population that believes in the legitimacy of what it pays into.

Parma's tradition of self-governance runs deep, forged in the era of the Italian communes when the city fought alongside its neighbors to defend their liberties against imperial ambition. We draw on this inheritance to structure the relationship between the crown and our urban communities, offering protections and recognized rights in exchange for the taxes and soldiers that sustain the state. This compact roots our authority in consent as much as in force, making our government a more stable and cooperative partner for all who live under it.

The Bishop of Parma has long wielded an authority that rivals the secular power in this city, guiding its spiritual life through some of the most remarkable religious buildings in northern Italy. We choose to align ourselves with this institution rather than resist it, channeling its influence toward the stability and devotion of our people. This partnership between crown and church strengthens the faith of our subjects and gives our government a source of moral authority that no military force can easily replace.

The elevation of our city to the capital of an independent realm marks a new chapter for Parma — no longer a possession passed between greater powers, but the seat of a recognized territorial state with its own traditions and ambitions. We move quickly to establish the institutions and ceremonies of sovereignty, giving our subjects a clear identity and our neighbors a clear interlocutor. This consolidation of legitimate authority makes our state harder to absorb and easier to govern.

Parma will be transformed into a laboratory for theatrical wonder, culminating in the construction of the first permanent proscenium theater. By establishing the picture-frame stage, Parma will create a literal and symbolic boundary between the audience and the divine artifice of performance. Our obsession with the scena — integrating complex hydraulics and ingenious pulley systems — will elevate opera from an academic experiment into a supreme spectacle of state power. This architectural breakthrough will turn us into a global magnet for scenographers, setting the technical standard for the modern opera house.

The cured hams and aged wheels of cheese produced in the lowlands around our city have become luxury goods traded across the continent, arriving in courts and counting houses as emblems of the finest the Po plain can offer. We protect and formalize the production of these goods, regulating the standards that make them exceptional and ensuring their export enriches our treasury as much as it delights our customers. This reputation for culinary excellence turns a humble agricultural tradition into a lasting source of commercial and diplomatic prestige.

A generation of reformers has convinced our court that the old machinery of government — its privileges, its exemptions, its slow customary procedures — is an obstacle to the welfare of our subjects rather than for their protection. We systematically replace custom with codified law, bringing reason to bear on taxation, education, and the management of public affairs. This commitment to rational governance makes our state more efficient, our laws more predictable, and our subjects more willing to trust that the government works in their interest.

Before we had painted our greatest canvases or trained our most celebrated condottieri, we had already declared our ambition in water and stone — the Fontana Maggiore, sculpted by Nicola and Giovanni Pisano and fed by a new aqueduct the whole commune funded, rising at the heart of Perugia as proof that no city in central Italy was richer, prouder, or more capable of collective ambition. The fountain gathered every saint, every trade good, and every classical virtue into a single monument and said with marble what no charter could say as well. This civic statement draws pilgrims and merchants to our center and tightens our hold over the streets they fill.

Pietro Vannucci — the Perugino — built the most admired workshop in Umbria within our walls, and his students fanned across Italy carrying the grace of the Umbrian style wherever commissions took them. Raphael came here to learn at his feet before Rome claimed the greater man, and the city that taught the teacher of Raphael carries an artistic reputation no rival in our region can easily dismiss. This tradition of workshop teaching and intensive apprenticeship makes our city a magnet for painters, patrons, and the steady flow of commissions that follows wherever skilled hands gather.

Our city's emblem is the Griffin, and nowhere has it been carried further than on the banners of the Baglioni condottieri who sold their swords — and won wars — across the length of the peninsula. Perugia produces soldiers the way Florence produces painters — in quantity, at quality, with an instinct for command honed by centuries of factional street-fighting and seasonal raiding. This martial tradition breeds officers who inspire loyalty and soldiers who hold their nerve when less experienced men break.

When the Pope imposed his salt monopoly, our people took up whatever weapons lay to hand — hence the papal mockery that named our uprising the Guerra delle Forche, the War of the Forks. We lost that war and were humiliated — the Baglioni expelled, the Rocca Paolina built directly over their palaces as a stone declaration of contempt — yet the defeat calcified into something more durable than pride. This bone-deep suspicion of outside authority makes every Perugian hill a natural fortress and every invader understand that whatever they take from us will cost more to hold than any strategic advantage can justify.

Long after our political independence was absorbed into the Papal States, the Accademia del Disegno and the learned societies we maintained under papal patronage kept our intellectual and artistic culture alive — training the officials, theorists, and artists who staffed institutions far beyond our own borders. Every great power on the peninsula knew that Perugian training produced reliable men, and the steady demand for our graduates made our academies prosperous even as our political leverage diminished. This tradition of practical learned culture sharpens every instrument of governance we exercise and ensures our city punches above its political weight in the councils that matter.

When revolution swept across Italy, our ancient university responded not by retreating into its medieval privileges but by opening its doors to the sons of merchants and artisans who would carry the new politics forward. The faculty of the Università degli Studi di Perugia produced the lawyers and pamphlet writers who made the Risorgimento possible in Umbria, turning a scholastic institution into an engine of civic transformation. This capacity to translate learning into organization means that no reform our government wishes to pursue will lack for educated men who know how to carry it out.

For generations, our mountain lords levied troops on custom and season, calling men to arms when the harvest was done and sending them home before the first snow. We have replaced this improvised tradition with a formal ordinance that fixes the size, equipment, and training standards of our infantry and binds our cities and rural lords to consistent obligations that can be called on at any time. This Ordinansa Piemontèisa (Ordinanza Piemontese in standard Italian: Piedmontese Ordinance) gives our army a professional core that holds its cohesion between campaigns, advancing the discipline and tradition of arms that lesser levies can never maintain.

The plains of the Po where they open onto our territory have long supported a class of lesser noble horsemen whose wealth depended on the quality of their horses and the reputation of their lance arm. We have organized these scattered men-at-arms into a formal cavalry, standardizing their equipment and training in coordinated maneuver rather than the individual charge that served in an earlier age. This Cavalleria Piemontese can screen our flanks, pursue a broken enemy, and fight in the loose formations that modern battlefield conditions demand, giving our armies a mobility that infantry alone cannot provide.

The ancient road descending from the Alpine passes into the Po plain once carried the legions of Rome; it has never ceased to carry merchants, envoys, and armies for whom the Piedmontese corridor is the most direct route between Italy and the north. We invest in the maintenance and security of these roads, building waypoints and toll stations that bring reliable revenue and ensure that goods in transit can move faster through our territory than through any rival route. This control over the Via d'le Gàlie (Via delle Gallie in standard Italian: Road of the Gauls) makes us an indispensable link in the chain of European commerce, increasing the capacity of our markets and giving our envoys natural openings at the courts that depend on the roads we manage.

A generation of engineers trained on the latest Italian treatises on fortification has surveyed every significant town in our domain and begun the work of converting the old circuit walls into a network of modern bastions — angled, low, and wide enough to mount artillery while denying the enemy any approach that our own guns cannot cover. We tie these citadels together by road and signal, so that a garrison threatened in one valley can expect support from the next. This Sistema delle Cittadelle transforms Piedmont into a country that cannot be overrun but must be taken fortress by fortress, a prospect that gives even the most determined aggressor pause before crossing our borders.

The generation of reformers who have gathered around our court have convinced us that the task of government is not merely to preserve what exists but to discover what works better and systematically replace the old with the new. We open our administration to men trained in the academies and experimental societies of the age, commission reports on everything from agricultural yields to judicial procedure, and fund the education of a class of administrators who can read a budget as readily as a treaty. This Còrt Ëluminà (Corte Illuminata in standard Italian: Enlightened Court) produces a state whose institutions are continuously improved by reason rather than paralyzed by custom, making our government faster, our research more productive, and our subjects more literate.

The combination of water power from our mountain rivers, a growing population of skilled artisans in our cities, and the raw materials of the Alpine foothills has created the conditions for an early industrial transformation that no other region of Italy can yet match. We invest in the hydraulic mills, the standardized workshops, and the credit institutions that allow this productive base to expand systematically rather than grow by accident. This Base Industriale generates income from activities that were once invisible to the treasury and draws workers from the countryside into our towns, building the urban population and the taxable wealth of our state together.

Our oasis sits at the confluence of three trans-Saharan caravan routes (the western route to Tafilalt and Sijilmasa, the central route to Ouargla and the Niger, and the eastern route to Ghadāmis and Tripoli), making us the natural meeting-point for caravans of every Maghrebi state. Our central market draws traders from Tunis, Algiers, Fez, Tripoli, and the deep-Sahara every season, and the migrant families who follow the caravans settle in our growing urban quarters. This crossroads geography gives our state a trade-route reach across the entire Saharan network and a steady urban migration draw that no single-route oasis can match.

Our crown raises a permanent military garrison through caravan-tax revenues. The zakāt al-'ushūr on incoming goods funds standing oasis-guard companies and a tribal-cavalry reserve drawn from the surrounding Berber confederations. Our tribesmen serve in rotation on the city walls and at the caravan-staging waterholes, earning a share of caravan-fees in lieu of regular pay, and our crown's permanent military establishment grows independent of either central-Algerian or Tunisian tributary demands. This caravan-funded levy system gives our state a permanent garrison force at no fiscal cost to the regular agricultural economy.

The Beni Djellab family proclaim themselves Sultans of Touggourt, consolidating power over the Souf and Wādī Rīgh oasis-complexes under a single dynastic line whose dynastic continuity outlasts every neighboring oasis-confederation. They build the central Touggourt qaṣr as both ceremonial residence and administrative center, organize a makhzen-style chancery for fiscal records, and project authority across the surrounding ksūr through marriage-alliances and military levies. This sultanate institution gives the Souf oasis-region a centralized political form that the consensus-governed neighboring oases never achieve.

Our Sultan negotiates a careful autonomy from the Algerian Ottoman Regency, recognizing the Sublime Porte's nominal suzerainty, paying a modest annual tribute, and accepting periodic Janissary detachments from Algiers as garrison auxiliaries, while retaining full internal governance and an independent fiscal apparatus. Our court hires Christian renegades, Andalusi exiles, and Ottoman Janissaries on contractual terms alongside our Berber tribal levies, giving our military a cosmopolitan officer-corps no purely-tribal sultanate can field. This negotiated autonomy preserves our independence through centuries of Algerian-Regency political turbulence.

Our Beni Djellab sultans refine the makhzen administrative apparatus into a proper fiscal institution, registering palm-groves and date-yields, recording caravan transactions, paying salaried scribes and judges from a central treasury, and dispensing justice through a tiered court system from the village qāḍī up to the sultan's own dīwān. We hire trained administrators from Tunis, Algiers, and even Cairo as advisors, our court correspondence in formal Arabic flows out across the Ottoman world, and our archives preserve every fiscal record of the sultanate. This administrative sophistication gives our state a fiscal and judicial reach unique among Saharan oasis-polities.

Our central oasis hosts the principal Qādiriyya Sufi zwāyā of the southern Algerian Sahara (Tolga, Sidi Khaled, and the chain of lodges between), drawing pilgrims from every oasis between the Aurès and the Sahel, and binding the southern religious establishment to our court through shared ritual and endowed land. Our sultan funds the upkeep of the lodge mosques, the teaching circles of the Qādiriyya shayḵs, and the seasonal mawlid festivals that draw thousands of pilgrims to our city. This Sufi-network patronage gives our crown a religious-cultural soft-power reach across the south that no purely secular sultanate can match.

We rule these hilltop towns and valleys as lords whose authority is ancient and whose right to govern has never been successfully challenged. Our people know that the Montefeltro have always defended their lands and their customs, and that loyalty has built a bond between lord and subject stronger than any decree. This seignory is not merely power over a territory but a compact that both sides have chosen to honor.

The hilltops of our domain have been fortified over many generations, turning every elevated town into a position that would take a determined army weeks to reduce. Our soldiers learn their craft on these steep approaches and defend positions where a small garrison can hold off a much larger force. The Hill Fortress network of our territory is both our shield and the school in which our military tradition is trained.

Our court has been called the most perfectly ordered in all of Italy, and men of learning and artistic ambition travel great distances to take part in its life. The conversations, performances, and works of art we foster here have inspired accounts of what a Perfect Court might look like, and those accounts have spread our reputation far beyond our borders. This refinement of governance and culture is the greatest thing we have built.

We have nurtured a tradition of mathematical and philosophical inquiry that has made our city known throughout Europe for the precision of its thinkers. The Mathematical School of our court has produced translations, commentaries, and original works that advance the sciences and win us admiration from the finest universities. This commitment to learning opens our citizens' minds and sharpens our capacity to understand and shape the world.

The potters and painters of our city have developed a tradition of tin-glazed maiolica whose vivid colors and intricate scenes are sought by collectors and courts across the continent. Our ceramic guilds guard and transmit their techniques across generations, ensuring that the quality which made our name endures. This craft industry exports our culture in every painted dish and decorated vessel that leaves our workshops.

Our university has endured through changes of government and the upheavals of the ages, continuing to draw students and scholars to our city by the reputation of its teaching. The long tradition of learning established in our most glorious days has become a living institution that carries that spirit forward into a new era. This continuity of scholarship is our gift to the future and our connection to the greatness of our past.

u.t: Chivalric order: Society with the Donkey

adv.d: Founded to protect knightly interests within the Empire, the Gesellschaft mit dem Esel has entrenched itself in the lands surrounding Heidelberg. Their expertise in governance, as well as their ability to sponsor tourneys, will improve our cultural standing.

The rulers of Cephalonia and Zante have developed a long tradition of raiding any enemy vessel foolish enough to sail without adequate protection through the Ionian approaches. These island-based raids amass considerable wealth through plunder and ransom while simultaneously weakening our enemies' naval logistics in the western Aegean, thereby allowing the tiny county to punch far above its weight and preserve its independence.

As the lords of Cephalonia, Zante, and Ithaca, we sit at the crossroads of the Adriatic and the Mediterranean, acting as the first line of defense for Italy. Our naval strategy focuses on 'Anti-Access' warfare, using heavy fortifications and fast scouting vessels to deny the enemy the ability to harbor in the Ionian Isles. We are the gatekeepers of the West, and no fleet enters the Adriatic without our silent consent.

The unique climate of the Ionian Islands allows for the mass cultivation of the Zante currant, a luxury dried fruit that has become a staple of European diets. By dominating the production and export of this niche crop, we have created a specialized economic engine that generates vast wealth for a relatively small territory. The 'Currant Lords' of Cephalonia are among the wealthiest nobles in the Latin East.

adv.n: The Chancery of the Three Tongues
adv.d: Our administration has evolved to issue all decrees in Latin, Greek, and Italian, reflecting the diverse merchant and noble classes of the Ionian Isles. This linguistic inclusivity attracts high-value migrants from the mainland and the Italian peninsula who seek a stable, multi-cultural legal environment. It effectively reduces the friction of governance in a sea of diverse identities.

We have transformed the natural deep-water bay of Argostoli into a premier naval refitting station. Unlike the massive Arsenals of Venice, ours specializes in the rapid repair of small-tonnage vessels like brigantines and galiots used for Aegean raiding. This specialized infrastructure keeps our fleet at sea longer than our rivals, ensuring local naval superiority.

We have granted extensive privileges to our local merchants, allowing them to form self-governing trade companies that manage the most lucrative exports and imports. This mercantile autonomy has fostered a wealthy urban class that bankrolls the County's modern administrative reforms.

Through a masterclass in marital diplomacy and unwavering loyalty to the Holy Roman Emperors, we have risen from local lords to Princes of the Holy Roman Empire. By securing marriage ties to the thrones of our neighbors, we have positioned ourselves as the indispensable 'Shield of the South'. This meteoric rise grants us the prestige to demand respect from the greatest of European houses.

Before we were Princes of the Empire, the House of Cilli was defined by the sharp blades of the Sanneck knights. By leading elite mercenary companies for the Hungarian and Imperial crowns in the fields of Dalmatia and Italy, we have turned the 'contract of war' into a tool for dynastic elevation. This tradition of professional military service allows us to field superior sellswords at a fraction of the cost.

Following our deep involvement in the successions of our neighbors, we formalize our legal claims to oversee the southern frontier of the Empire as the primary protectors of the realm. Even as our rivals attempt to absorb our lands, the administrative structures and 'Imperial Immediate' status we have secured ensure that our territory remains a privileged hub of regional governance.

As the primary lords of the southern frontier, we have transformed our estates into a permanent military supply chain. By patronizing the ironworks of the Savinja Valley, we ensure our heavy cavalry and border guards are equipped with the finest plate and firearms forged in Inner Austria. This localized military industry reduces our reliance on foreign armaments and keeps our regiments battle-ready at all times.

To reflect our status as Princes of the Empire, we have invited Italian architects to redesign our urban centers in the grand Baroque style. These sprawling palaces and public squares are not merely for show; they serve as centralized administrative hubs where the state's bureaucracy is professionalized. The sheer splendor of our capital serves to overawe foreign diplomats and domestic rivals alike, cementing our legitimate right to rule.

Our ancestral valleys have been transformed from a feudal pastoral land into the industrial heartbeat of our realm. We have seized this momentum by establishing massive industries, alongside modern steam-powered mills that process the raw timber and iron of the surrounding mountains. This rapid modernization has created a new class of skilled laborers and engineers, turning our capital into a center of technological innovation that propels the entire state into the industrial age.

Our oases (Tozeur, Nefta, Douz, El Hamma, and the smaller settlements of the Chott) serve as one of the last refuges of the Ibāḍiyya tradition in the eastern Maghreb, sheltering Khārijī-Ibadi survivors from the doctrinal conflicts of the early Islamic centuries. Our clergy maintains the distinctive Ibadi fiqh alongside the surrounding Mālikī majority, preserving a tolerance and a religious autonomy unusual in the Sunni-dominated regions. This Ibadi tolerance and clergy-establishment foundation gives our oases a religious resilience that purely-Mālikī oases cannot match.

The local Sufi marabouts of the Djerid, combining Ibadi religious orthodoxy with practical wisdom in oasis water-rights, palm-grove inheritance, and caravan-protection ritual, anchor the religious-judicial life of our oasis cities through their permanent lodges and seasonal pilgrimage festivals. Our crown endows the shrines of the great founding shayḵs and patronizes the teaching circles of their living successors. This Ibadi-Sufi synthesis gives our religious establishment a depth and a moral-authority legitimacy across the southern oases that purely-imported orders cannot match.

Our central madrasa at Tozeur — funded by the assembled palm-grove rentier families and staffed by Ibadi and Mālikī teachers in equal measure — trains the scribes, judges, and missionaries of our oases through a curriculum that mediates between the two madhāhib and the broader Saharan scholarly tradition. Our graduates serve as qādīs across the Djerid, our students travel to Tunis and Cairo for advanced training, and our reputation for cross-doctrinal scholarship attracts pilgrim-students from beyond our territory. This concentrated scholarly authority gives our state a clergy-literacy ceiling and a religious-conversion reach across the southern oases that purely-rural Ibadi communities cannot replicate.

Our oasis-confederation negotiates a careful autonomy from the central Tunis court, recognizing Hafsid sovereignty in name, paying a modest annual date-tribute, and accepting periodic inspection visits, while retaining full internal governance, water-rights jurisprudence, and an independent religious establishment. Our diplomatic envoys negotiate as equals at the Tunis court, our merchant houses maintain factor-relationships in the coastal cities, and our oases avoid the costly direct integration that flatland frontier-confederations suffer. This negotiated autonomy reduces the antagonism we receive from the central court and lets our treasury retain a court-spending efficiency the directly-administered oases cannot keep.

Each of our oasis-cities is governed by its own majlis al-jamā'a (assembly of palm-grove owning family heads, religious shayḵs, and merchant guild representatives), meeting at the central mosque-courtyard to debate civic affairs, settle inheritance and water-rights disputes, and elect the chief-judge for each ceremonial year. The assembly governance has no inherited royal offices; authority flows through consensus and from the legitimacy of the religious-scholarly establishment. This consensus governance gives our oasis-confederation a cabinet-efficiency and a stability-resilience rooted in religious-communal solidarity that no autocratic court can easily match.

Our late-period intellectuals revive the publishing of the great Ibadi-Wahbī classical works (the legal commentaries of ath-Thamīnī, the spiritual poetry of the Djerid mystics, and the chronicles of the southern Tunisian oases) alongside reformist Arabic newspapers connecting our community to the wider Ibadi world from Mzab to Oman and Zanzibar. Our bilingual periodicals circulate from Tozeur through Gabes to Tunis, and our scholars correspond on equal terms with the Cairo and Damascus reformist press. This Ibadi-heritage revival binds our scattered oasis tradition into a shared modern identity and gives our state a books-output reach and a prestige standing that the smaller Ibadi communities elsewhere cannot match.

The fortress of Athlone, standing astride the mighty river Shannon, is the key to controlling the heart of Ireland. The O'Kellys of Hy Many, long-standing lords of these lands, have fought fiercely to defend their holdings against Norman incursions.
We are surrounded by weakly defended territories ripe for the taking! Let us send out some adventurous courtiers to enforce our authority in these unclaimed lands.
The Paik System is a corvée labor system where capable adults, the so-called Paiks, are obligated to serve in the state militia in exchange for farmland.
Paiks are foot soldiers of India who are renowned for their offensive and defensive versatility and their skill in archery.

Paiks are foot soldiers of India who are renowned for their offensive and defensive versatility and their skill in archery. As the weapons develop, so does their portfolio of skills. Thus, the bows of the early eras have been replaced by the modern musket, yet their versatility still prevails.

u.t: Chivalric order: Society with the Lion

adv.d: Founded in the woes of the Western Schism, the Löwenbund is sworn to protect our lands from heretical revolts. We should grant them our official sponsorship and incorporate them into our court to further our cause.

Our Order is named the Knights Hospitaller for a reason: we were originally the protective force of a pilgrims' hospital in Jerusalem. Though Jerusalem is lost to the Saracens, we still provide medical aid to those in need, including our brave knights, who heartily return to the battlefield much faster than most armies.

b: War with No Casus Belli Cost: -5%
adv.d: We have been driven from Acre and Cyprus, but the Order of the Hospital of St. John will retreat no further. In pagan times, a Colossus stood sentinel over the harbor of Rhodes, but today, the greatest fortifications the world has ever known have taken up the guard!

Our Order was formed by faithful souls from every nation in Christendom. This fact, combined with our need for external support to fulfill our missions, have made us adept at recruiting helping hands for our cause. We will take advantage of our omnipresence in Europe to reach the ears of powerful catholic_adj rulers, and sway them to our side.

In our frequent clashes with fierce foreign corsairs, the thought has occurred to us that these scurvy dogs might have the right idea about looting and pillaging the coast, but they are preying on the wrong targets. Piracy may be a vile sin in peacetime, but in times of war, it is known as 'privateering,' and that is another thing altogether.

Knights of our Order were present in the wars against Saladin and defended the last Outremer Crusader outpost, Acre. If any among us needs inspiration to do heroic deeds, they need to look only at what the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St. John have accomplished in the past. The name Knights Hospitaller is truly eternal, as is our famed courage in battle.

The famed Turkish privateer Hayreddin Barbarossa fought many legendary encounters against the Knights, but he was hardly the only corsair we have encountered. Turkish raiding and looting of all of Southern Europe, tolerated by the Barbary states and funded by the Turks, must end. The Knights will do their job protecting innocent sailors at any cost.

As long as any faithful Catholic is in danger of religious persecution, our mission is not over! Be it during a pilgrimage to the Tomb of our Lord and Savior, or while crossing the seas and fending off corsairs, we will never stop training and never rest, ready to leap into combat at a moment's notice.

The Reformation has harmed our cause as knights from Germany and Scandinavia have started murmuring questions about the nature of the Communion Host, but the always-present Turkic threat has a way of making such disputes seem minor. Perhaps we should focus on defending the realm, and debate theology once the Saracen threat is safely at bay?

While our Order's principal duty is to fight, we serve our people in other ways as well. Over the centuries, we have developed the art of rapid construction, erecting buildings and fortifications with remarkable speed. We will use this expertise to make our capital into both an impregnable fortress, and a dynamic center of culture.

adv.n: The Right Hand of the Pope
adv.d: As time goes on, and the Crusades start to fade from the memory of our people, the importance of having the Pope's ear increases. We ingratiate ourselves until we are the closest confidantes to the Supreme Pontiff. Naturally, our devotion to his service will benefit us enormously — and why not enjoy our hard-won privileges?

The world evolves, and those who fail to adapt are forgotten by history. Our Order has endured for over half a millennium, and we will not fade away now! Our mortal bodies will eventually join the Creator, but our Order must first become immortal. We will transform ourselves into the most modern nation of our age, strengthening ourselves from the very core.

While some nations are often described as an Army with a State, we, on the other hand, have always been an Order with a nation, ever since our acquisition of Rhodes from the Greeks. Nevertheless, we cannot help but admire how efficiently they have harnessed their resources to become a formidable nation. Inspired by their success, we will implement reforms to ensure our military can confront any adversary with confidence.

ref.d: As our focus changed from defending castles in the Holy Land to fighting pirates and heathens on the seas, we had to change the way our Order operates. Galleys now will be our battlefields, and our first bulwarks against the enemies of Christ.
